A little over a year ago I decided to stick my toe in the HiRes Digital Audio pool.
I didn’t have a boat load of Benjamin’s to sink into the endeavor but I did get the best my budget could afford.
I got the HiBy R6 DAP and two IEM’s to go with it.
The TinAudio T2’s and the BGVP DMG’S.
Both are outstanding IEM’s but I had been hearing a lot of buzz about the hybrid electrostatic/DD Tin P1’s and was seriously considering going that way.
The T2’s were a good buy and the P1’s were getting great reviews from uToobers I trust.
Then about a month ago these BQEYZ Spring 1’s hit the market and the buzz shifted.
I decided to give them a spin.
If they weren’t a big enough improvement over the BGVP’s I could always return ‘em.
Well they ain’t going anywhere.
The advances in personal audio over the course of the last year have been remarkable.
I’m not a big fan of Chinese stuff but they are getting a solid reputation for two of the markets I dabble in, HiRes Audio and folding knives.
As for these Spring 1’s they f*ing rock.
Amazing soundstage, crisp punchy bass, outstanding mids and perfectly fine highs (I say perfectly fine because I have tinnitus and my hearing craps out at about 15kHz).
Every instrument has its place and is distinct.
The first thing I listened to was Pink Floyd Meddle and it nearly brought tears to my eyes.
For an investment of just under $200 (I got the 16 core silver cable upgrade, although the stock one is perfectly adequate) you really can’t go wrong.

Can’t wait for next year.

I did have the opportunity to compare these with the Shuoer Tape hybrid IEM’s and it only took me about t minutes to box up the Tape’s and return them.
The Tape’s were much brighter and lacking the warmth and soundstage of the Spring 1’s.
Of course as with everything that is as subjective as audio YMMV.

It works, but TERRIBLE tray design The Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure that I received works, but the tray design is really quite awful.

I'm not going to return it, but the next time I buy a 3.5 inch HDD USB enclosure I will look elsewhere.

I own both the Thermaltake Max 5G (USB3) & Max 4 (USB2) HDD enclosures.
I also have worked with one of the Sabrent "fan-ed" USB HDD enclosures.

I cannot remember if it was USB 2 or 3.

The Sabrent enclosure was pretty good, other than the fact that the enclosure box "slid around" in its stand (the part that contacts the table/shelf).

The Thermaltake enclosures are the best and most everything about them is top notch.
Unfortunately, Thermaltake no longer manufactures this sort of enclosure.
They do still make BlacX USB docks.

Those are docks, not enclosures.

Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure
------------------------------------------

First come the complaints.

Rosewill provided incorrect HDD screws/bolts.
When working with PCs there are normally only 2 types of screws/bolts = coarse thread and fine thread.
HDDs take coarse thread screws.
The 4 screws the Rosewill provided looked like coarse thread screws, but they wouldn't go into my HDDs more then a couple of turns.

I threw them out and used my own screws.

At this point I have tried 3 different 3.5 inch HDDs with the Rosewill RX304 enclosure and none of the HDDs were able to become fully seated within the HDD tray.
By fully seated I mean that all 4 HDD screw holes line up with the screw holes of the HDD tray.
I was never able to get more than 2 screws in.

I used WD and Seagate HDDs.

But before trying to align the screw holes you have to get the HDD into the tray in the 1st place.
THIS IS VERY DIFFICULT TO DO because the tray (at the top) is ever so slightly narrower then the HDD that is going into it.
WhiskeyTangoFoxtrot???
I guess that I should try bending the tray wall outwards to make it permanently wider.
As a buyer I'm supposed to doing this kind of BS maneuver?
This is a very bad joke ... and it is on me.
If I bend the tray wall outwards will I break something?

The mechanical engineer that designed this tray is going to hell when they die.

OK.
So now the HDD is in the tray (with only 2 screws) and the SATA cables are attached.

The SATA cable attachments are a whole other mediocre story, but they can be made to work, so we will continue.

One (or more) reviewer/s suggested that the air passage that remains after seating the HDD is not wide enough for decent air flow to the fan and then out of the case.

I could be wrong, but I suspect that there is is just enough space for reasonable air flow.

Second comes the reasonably good part.

Once the HDD is in the tray and the tray (plus interface board) is reinserted into the enclosure box you can put the end on and attach it with 2 screws.
This part of the procedure is OK, but nowhere near top quality.
There is an internal rail inside the enclosure box that aligns the HDD/tray/interface board within said box.

But, there are only 2 "keys" in the frame that go into the rail, so the HDD tray assembly is sorta slip/sliding around in the box until you get it fully inserted, at which time the end edge of the enclosure box mates up with an internal channel in the plastic front end.

So now we have the box fully assembled, and we put it in its stand (4 rubber "nubs" keep the box from slipping around, nice).

We then cable up the enclosure's power and connect the USB 3 to a computer.

Once all of the above is done you get pretty good performance.
On a 2 TB HDD I was able to read the outside tracks at 200 MB/sec.
That's the same performance that I get with that HDD inside a computer cabled directly to the mobo.

The USB 3 interface worked well for me.

On a slightly down note the program HDDScan could not read the SMART values through the interface board of the Rosewill RX304, but was able to read the SMART values through the interface board of a 2.5 inch Mediasonic USB 3 enclosure that I also own.

Other programs may well be able to "penetrate" this USB interface to get SMART data ... who knows.

As I said at the start the Rosewill RX304 is OK, but I won't be buying any more of these units.

Not as effective as standard dipole antenna I have a steel roof home, which hinders the FM reception on my HD Radio receiver.
Up until now I'd been piggy backing my reception off my flat Mohu TV window antenna with an amplifier.
Note this window does not face the broadcast towers.

But last week I realized my antenna had an FM trap, so I was excited try a switch to the Terk.

Unfortunately, the Terk doesn't perform as well as the Mohu, even using the amplifier and experimenting with different placements.
However, I was motivated to revisit my old  dipole wire antenna and use it with the amp.
To my surprise, when experimenting with positioning, the dipole performed better than either of the newer antennas.

I'd say about 1-2 bars better on my 5 bar meter, depending on which antenna I'm using, and the station.

I suppose the Terk would be okay if you have a good signal and want a modern looking antenna.
However, for my needs, the dipole antenna does a better job.

Mid-Range Quality At A High-End Price When you order a $400 pair of headphones the last thing that you expect is for the manufacturer to take a bunch of shortcuts on quality, but this high-end pair of Technics headphones seem to be full of compromises and it almost seems like the company put more effort into marketing and packaging than it did in the final product.

The biggest letdown with this product is it's construction.
It's almost entirely made of plastic, which is something that you might expect from a pair of $35 Bluetooth headphones, but not ones that sell for nearly $400.

Obviously, the headphone is not going to be covered under warranty if the plastic construction breaks, and since it is mostly plastic, that is what is most likely to break first.

The other big compromises are the lack of the latest in Bluetooth technology, which is Bluetooth 5.0.
There are plenty of headphones selling for far under $100 that use Bluetooth 5.0.
Why not these?
Charging is another issue.
Rather than a fast charging USB-C connection or a convenient wireless charging connection there is a cheap and antiquated Micro-USB charger input.
Again, fine for a cheap pair of headphones, but when you are talking about $400 headphones you expect MUCH better.
The ear pads are also less comfortable than I would expect in this price class.

They aren't horrible, but do not have the ultra soft, leather-like feel to them that you expect in high-end headphones.

On to the good things about these headphones...
The packaging is really nice.
If only the product was designed as well as the packing I would be so happy with this product.
Bluetooth connectivity is flawless, but most $20 Bluetooth products can say the same.
The ANC feature is both flexible and powerful.
They do a great job at blocking out outside noise without affecting audio quality.

From my limited experience with ANC headphones, these are the best I have tried thus far.

The audio quality is also quite impressive for a Bluetooth device.
While it does not produce he best sound I have ever heard from a pair of corded headphones they are on par with the best Bluetooth headphones I have used.

I would hesitate to say that they are THE best sounding Bluetooth headphones I have used though.

While these are "nice" Bluetooth headphones they come nowhere near what I would expect from something in this price class.
They are about on par with what you would expect for a pair of Bluetooth headphones selling in the $180-$200 range, but that's it.
The lack of latest features and the use of plastic throughout it's construction really rubs me the wrong way.
If these sold at half of their current price I might give them a four star review.
I think that I am being generous at giving them the three stars that they are getting though.

Ignore Description Though This outlet strip works o.k.
Just don't take the description of the product too seriously.
For one thing, it claims to provide a total of 2.4 Amps to each of it's 4 charging ports, but provides a total of only 4.2 Amps.
Even a third grader can tell you that 2.4 x 4 is more than 4.2.
So, the total amount of Amps per port is only about half of what is claimed.

So, you can pretty much forget fast charging any of your devices if you have more than 3 items charging at the same time.

I'm not sure about the claim of the 2 AC outlets having "supper wide space".
Maybe it means that you get more space while eating dinner?
It also claims to feature "4 smart Micro USB ports".
Nope.

They are just regular sized USB ports, not micro, which would make no sense anyway.

Other than that, this "power strip", as they call it, is pretty unremarkable.
It is missing a great number of functions that you would expect, even in it's price range.

Some of the features that it does NOT include are: NO surge protection or line filtering, NO reset switch, NO on/off switch, No ability for the plug to swivel positions, NO LED to show if the charger outlets are working, NO clamps along the side of the unit to coil the cord around.

NO warranty beyond 30 days and NO company contact information.

So, it's basically just a cheaply constructed Chinese product with only 2 AC outlets and maybe 2 outlets that will quick charge your phone at the same time.
Nothing too exciting here.

I would recommend it based on my short experience.

I hooked up one unit as instructed and updated firmware and measured my up and down speed.
I have a real basic internet speed so I know this unit is capable of doing more.
I used the same speedtest off the web for all my tests for consistency.
In general, I found this unit to be as fast as my old (read, real old) unit in the same room and the room next door.
Two rooms down, this unit is not strong as a dedicated router and speeds began to drop.
So, I added the second unit in the basement (I couldn't tell much difference between ethernet backhaul versus wifi but I think that has a lot to do with my basic internet package from my ISP.
I anticipate better results when I upgrade).
My third and final unit I felt wasn't even necessary.
Even the basement unit provided sufficient coverage in my upstairs bedroom which never worked with my single router.

CONs
- I did plug in some old flash sticks, which had difficulty connecting through the USB 3.0 ports.

If you hold them tight, or wiggle slightly, they seem to connect and come on line.
- I would have liked one extra USB-C port, and one less USB 3.0 port for my purposes, and because USB-C is becoming prevalent in future products.
Overall, I am happy with the purchase and would recommend the product even though it is more expensive that alternative adaptors.

Portable Travel Monitor - Sharp, portable, and simple I usually use a three monitor setup at my office, but picked this up for a second monitor to keep in my go bag to set up when working at a customer site.

I wanted a screen that was light, sharp and clear, and easy to set up, and picked this up to try.

The screen is sharp and clear. 1080p on a 15" screen is the same pixel density as my laptop.
Works fine in either portrait or landscape, no autodetecting so you have to change it in the OS if you want to rotate it.
Had a detection issue initially (defaulted to 640x480), but it has been at 1080p since.

Good viewing angles, colors stay consistent even viewed quite off center, it claims to be IPS and looks the part.

14.5" wide by 9" tall and 1/2" thick with the case on.
Weight is about 2.5lbs also with the case - which you need, as it is the stand as well, but the case is just under 1lb of that.
Compares very well to trying to carry a full size monitor.

The case is a protective full wraparound, magnetically held in place front and back when on, it is pretty secure from falling off completely, but does not provide any bottom cushioning when vertical in portrait orientation in a bag, so keep that in mind.

My laptop bag has some cushioning under the inner, should be fine there.

As a stand, the case does a good job as long as you set it up on a flat surface and have the case on the right way - one side is the inside and is softer, greyish, and grippier, and the other is more black and slick, and if you put it on backwards it looks like it is attached but doesn't work well at all.
Confused me for a bit the first time I took the case off and put it back on wrong.
Otherwise it is a fairly standard magnetic tablet case / stand.

It is ONLY attached by magnets though, so pretty easy to disconnect unintentionally if you are twisting it at all while moving it in the stand position.

Connectivity is primarily USB-C.
It has two ports, one is power only, the other is signal or both signal and power.
My Latitude E5570 can provide  power over the Thunderbolt / USB-C connector using the same cable as the video signal.

So just the USB-C to C connector in the bag and quick to connect / disconnect is perfect.

The micro HDMI cable and separate power supply and USB A-C cable for power will be useful a few times a year when traveling for fun and I want to bring this with the xbox - but that won't be a primary use, and holding a controller while staying at the right distance for this to be functional would not be perfect.

It has a speaker.
Volume and quality compare poorly to my laptop speakers, this is more of a checkbox feature.

I have no plans to use them.

It also comes with a plastic screen protector ready to install.
At this size it is nearly impossible to get one of those on without bubbles, and I tried but was unsuccessful in avoiding those.

But I don't see any real need for it anyway - the case protects it for travel, and this isn't a touchscreen to carry around, no matter how tablet like it looks.

Overall, it is meeting my need for a travel monitor quite well.
We'll see how TSA treats it the next time I hit the air, and how it holds up over time, but this is very good and quite affordable for what I needed today.
Only issue is I keep trying to treat it like a touch screen, which it is not, but I'll get used to that in time.

Great Value My primary A/V system is 15 years old but my plasma TV, amplifier, and surround sound speakers still provide excellent quality.
With that said, as I have purchased new input devices, I wound up with a daisy chain of HDMI and optical splitters  behind my television.
As my cables and splitters aged I found myself jiggling cables to make good connections.
The last straw was the death of my old ROKU and they no longer make one with an optical out.
I bought all new cables and the FERRISA 4x2 Matrix, hooked up all my equipment but somethings had sound but no video.
I thought  I needed help setting up the EDID switches so I called Amazon support.
They have a  very friendly support team, but even with changes to the EDID switches no change.
Amazon overnighted a new device because of the holidays coming up.
Still no luck, so Amazon asked if I would call the manufacturer for help.
Fiibest support was great!
We tried some changes to the EDID switches again with no success.
They asked me to send them a list of all my input device's resolution and my TV's resolution.
My TV is 780P.
Some of my peripherals were 780P but newer devices were 1080P.
I manually changed everything to 780P.
Eureka!
Everything worked. (780 & 1080 are both hi def).
The Matrix instructions tell you not to leave it turned on all the time so you would have to unplug the jack to power it down.
I suggested to Fiibest that they add a power switch.
I have slowly turned my house into a "Smart Home" with Amazon Echo devices and I simply set up an Echo outlet.
I just have to say "Alexa, turn on TV Matix" and it is done.
Long review... bottom line: If you have equipment that is all the same video resolution this switch is plug and play.
If you don't it is easy to manually change the resolution in the settings menu of your devices.
I'm very pleased with it.

The smaller model would max out around 200Mbps with most of the features turned off and hardware offload enabled.

Turning on the threat management significantly slows the device.

Ubiquiti has a higher end model (XG) that was pulled from the market due to problems for a bit.
I'm hoping they get that product back out and also add something in between this PRO model and the XG or bump the specs.

A gigabit connection couldn't run on this model and it's obvious that the PRO isn't powerful enough for heavy workloads even at 500Mbps.

I really like the management features on unifi gear and it's the big selling point.

It was pretty easy to upgrade from the smaller USG to the pro model also.

I do hope they get a slightly faster model out and consider upgrading to 2.5Gbps nbase-T connectivity so one doesn't have to jump to fiber connections for moderate performance.

If you were using a connection up to say 300Mbps, most of the features would work and you'd be pretty happy with this.

I just don't think it's ready for 500Mbps to gigabit speeds.

Finally, the IPv6 support on this device is mediocre.
Part of the problem is the upstream router from my cable provider, but the IPv6 supports feels like an afterthought and is a little irritating to try to setup.
Documentation is lacking in this area.
I can get an IP address on the WAN interface, but have never been able to get it to assign an IP to the inside network.
If you need IPv6 functionality, it might be better to go with another product.

Good product but some design flaws.
I'm a big fan of UAG products they never disappoint.
The workmanship on this product was best in class.

However, there were two design short comings that are causing some problems.

The first shortcoming is that when I put the case in my bag spine-down, just jostling the bag will cause the keyboard portion to slide towards the hinges which causes it to become "unclipped" from the front of the case which forces me to re-seat the keyboard back into the slot.

The remedy for this would be for a second set of clips to be molded into the plastic to ensure a sturdier grip onto the keyboard based.

The second shortcoming probably is more a trade-off than a shortcoming.
Although the transparent polycarbonate/acrylic top cover is great looking, it also acts as an insulator and contributes to the display overheating.
This is as much a design flaw that Microsoft has been criticized for but if you see yellowing around the edges of the display, overheating is a contributing cause.
When I take the cover off the display cools down and does recover.
However, from experience I know that means I am shortening the life of the display and all the components inside.

I'm willing to live with this trade-off as it is still better to protect the device but when I am using this in desktop mode with the Microsoft docking station at my desk, I always leave a fan to blow on the display.

UAG could improve upon this by using an open ribbed approach for the top half of the case allowing for the shell to be in direct contact with air.

All in all, I am satisfied with the product as there has yet to be another like it that performs any better.

Excellent Performance at a fantastic price point I purchased these earbuds in December and I have to say that I am very impressed with the overall sound quality and performance considering the $50 price point.
For the money, I don't believe that you can find a better pair of wireless earbuds in terms of sound reproduction, fit, and overall quality.
Sure, I could have paid more for Apple earbuds but the marginal increase in performance is not worth the extra cost.
The pairing is simple, steady, and reliable.
Battery life is about 3 hours on a single charge when I listen to music, which is on par with other earbuds and what I'd expect from a device that I wear at the gym and for short periods of time.
Midrange and highs are good (letter grade = B+), but overall bass performance is decent (letter grade B-) which really is as expected.
I am not sure how you can engineer solid bass performance into an earbud, so my expectations are modest and given that, the Anker product is a success.
My thoughts on overall sound quality are not curved to reflect earbuds as a class, but rather what this device sounds like in reference to any audio reproduction.

I have sampled Beats and Apple earbuds and honestly, none of them can replace true over the ear headphones, but that is not their intended purpose just as earphones cannot replicate the sound of reference speakers.
Calls are clear and the microphones do a great job reducing background noise (letter grade = A-).
In short - I strongly recommend this product and don't believe that anyone would have any reason to be disappointed with the purchase of this product.

Please Read!

I did some very thorough research online and some adventuring in stores, and I have confirmed the following:

Samsung HDTV models listed below require an "M8 - 1.25 x 43mm" bolt in the bottom two screw holes, which does not really exist outside of the internet and cannot be found in hardware stores.

Alternatively, you can go to a hardware store and use the slightly more popular "M8 - 1.25 x 45mm" bolt with very minor space between the Part F bracket and the TV back and still have a solid connection without issue, which is what I have done.
You can add a washer or two and the connection should be really solid.
I found my bolts at a LOWE'S store, and they were the only ones available.

If absolutely necessary and people cannot find either of these bolts, the "M8 - 1.25 x 50mm" size is almost just as comfortable of a fit as the 45mm, though now you have to expect a bit more wobble, unless you want to add about 6 washers.

When I went to LOWE'S, one of the employees there had created a list of TV models by Samsung that he's run into that require these bolts.

He explained all of the issues I have mentioned here - that there is no such thing as a 43mm bolt, unless it's custom made online somewhere, or if you cut the bolt yourself to size(which would be easier to do if you start with a 50mm bolt).
He also explained how people were being scammed on Amazon by people selling 43mm bolts but they were actually 45mm.
I took a photo of his list and wrote down all supported models in it.

Otherwise, people can go online and grab them on Amazon.
They're more expensive on Amazon though by a few dollars.
They're only a few cents in stores.

I bought a new Samsung 970 EVO  M.2 NVMe drive and wanted to install it in my older Asus motherboard.
I was already using an M.2 drive but it was a SATA drive.

I found out that my motherboard would not support the NVMe drive and I needed a way to get it on the PCIe bus.

This little card has done that for me.
The card came with two plates. (full size and half size)  It came disassembled but they do provide the screws.

They also provided a small Phillips screwdriver to assemble it with.

I am still running Windows 7 so I needed a driver from Samsung to get the drive to work. (no drivers specific to the card itself are needed) Before I installed the drivers, Windows attempted to install them and failed.

I had an unknown PCI Express device in Device Manager.

After I installed the drivers, everything worked great.
I used the data migration software from Samsung and copied my C: drive from my old 2.5" SATA SDD to this new super-fast NVMe drive.

It took less than 15 minutes to copy my 500GB of data on my boot drive.

I went to the BIOS and told it to boot from the Samsung 970 EVO and it has been working great ever since. (just set it up today)

I ran a few CrystalDiskMark benchmarks on the drive. and I get different results than other people are getting.

I actually got much faster results on the 4K QD32 tests but slower on the sequential read and write tests.

The Samsung Magician software told a different story than the CrystalDiskMark software.

It had the sequential reads at 3600MB per second. (what I would expect from the drive)

I am sharing the PCIe bus with a video card so even though I put the card in 16x slot, I believe it is running at 8x since the video card is in the other 16x slot.
Either way, it is screaming fast.
My computer boots much faster and games and programs load incredibly fast.
Photoshop loads so fast, it is like opening a browser.

Photoshop is up and usable in about 4 seconds. (older CS version) Outlook loads in about 1.5 seconds.

The card can hold two M.2 drives. (one B key and one M key) I do not know if you can use them both at the same time or not.

I didn't bother with the heatsink, thermal material or the rubber bands.
I ran the Samsung Magician software many times after lots of disk activity to monitor the temp.
It is right where it should be without any heatsink.

I have installed several of these drives right on the motherboard and I have never used any type of heatsink in the past.

I do not believe that Samsung recommends using anything on the drive but other manufacturers may.

Sound quality is surprisingly good for $11- highs are fairly clear and detailed, bass has decent power but lacks a ton of clarity, and the mids are kinda lost in between the two.
The overall sound profile makes these good for heavier music like rock and metal, but might not work for everyone's taste.
For the price, though, it's hard to nitpick too hard.
Nice Wireless Headphones- Terrible Active Noise Cancellation.
As listening headphones, these are great.

Build quality is solid, padding in nice and gentle for extended listening periods, and the buttons are nice and tactile.

Sound quality is pretty good, if a bit soft.
Highs are nice and clear, mids are a little lacking, and bass is really empty.
Generally I'd say it's an energetic kind of sound, but it feels a little flat and hollow.

That's not necessarily a terrible thing, this makes for far more pleasant listening than the really warm bass heavy drivers you typically get in cheaper headphones, but it does mean that for heavier genres like rock or metal, you might find your music sounding a bit anemic.

The ANC is where these headphones fall apart.
Just don't flip that switch, don't bother.
The sealed closed back design works well enough for sound isolation, and IMO turning on the ANC actually enhances the noise rather than removes it.
I tested sitting in a room next to a standing fan- a constant tone.
The ANC turned that tone in a loud digital warble that made the noise much more annoying and harsh on the ears.
At normal listening volumes the design of the earcups alone killed most of the background noise anyway.
Surprisingly Good for the Price Much like its wired-only sibling, these headphones out of the box seem small and flimsy, but build quality is actually not terrible.

You're not expecting much, but the aesthetics are high quality, and it feels good enough to wear- so long as you realise the cups are small enough that they're on-ear, not over-ear.

What you get extra with the "Pro" version is of course bluetooth capability, as well as a surprisingly nice padded mesh carry bag.

Sound quality on this one is perhaps slightly worse than the wired-only Impulse headphones, with a sound signature that is a touch more bass heavy than even those were, and is a bit congested sounding, lacking clarity in the mids which can make the vocals indistinct at times.

Still, for the price these hold up very well.

Considering how slim the price difference is between these and the wired-only Impulse headphones, I'd say that go for these "Pro" headphones is basically a no-brainer if you're on a budget and can't afford anything in the next tier of quality.
Sounds Better Than It Looks Out of the box, my first reaction was "oh wow, these are the tiniest flimsiest children's headphones I've seen".
In the hands, the build quality isn't quite that bad, but it's not spectacular.
For the price, you can't expect much, and you don't get much.

The thinnest bare minimum "padding" on the top strap, some memory foam cups that are so small they sit on the ears, not over them, and wire friction adjustable mounts.

Sound quality is surprisingly good despite price and appearance though.
The sound is a bit warm, heavy in the bass, but is still fairly clear and holds up shockingly well in the mids and highs.
Vocals remain clear across a variety of genres.
Overally, for the money these are surprisingly decent value, I just would be very gentle with them as its clear that build quality was sacrificed for sound quality.
Okay Cheap Earbuds Like so many cheap headphones, the low end is overpowering, and the high end suffers.
Bass is strong but lacks detail, mids are okay, highs are soft.

Vocals will tend to get lost in music, and in general a lot of rock sounds messy and lacks distinction through these.

Build quality feels pretty good and solid with nice metal construction, though I worry about the longterm durability of the somewhat thin wires.
Decent Cheap Headphones Sound quality on these is quite good for how cheap they are.

Mids are present but soft, and the highs really get lost in the mix.

Sound quality is dreadful.

but I've tried a number of excellent wireless speakers and sports earbuds today in the $10-15 range which had much clearer sound than these.

Sound quality is a mixed bag.
Unlike a lot of cheap earbuds, these don't focus on the bass, instead they focus on the mids.
The trebel is very strong and overpowering, which gives weaks lows, and weak highs.
The overall effect is a sound that is sharp, but neutered.
Depending on the genre of music you prefer, and even the vocal range of the artists you prefer, these may work better or worse for you.

Size Can be Deceiving For something so small, you wouldn't expect much, but this thing punches above.

The first thing you notice picking it up is just how heavy it is!
It's crazy solid!

Combined with the silicone base (which unfortunately does collect dust like a magnet), this thing doesn't move when set on a table, even if its in a party and the table gets knocked around it sits SOLID.

In terms of sound, it's not a studio speaker, but for something so small you shouldn't expect it to be.
It gets decently loud before distortion, and it's got a decent sound.

It's heavy on treble and the upper end of bass... the lowest bass is lost, and the highs and vocals are a little soft, but overall the sound is a lot more distinct and clear than so many other speakers in this price range that go all in for bass and become muddy.
Solid Build, Cheap Sound The build quality on this is hard to argue with.
It feels built like a tank.

It's got a solid rubberised body, a nice beefy magnet for mounting on steel surfaces, a solid loop for hooking otherwise... the whole thing screams durability and usability.

Sound quality, however, really lets this down.
The speaker simply doesn't hold up to the price tag.
It's muddy, tinny, and muffled.
The bass is strong and punchy, but in the quest for making the lows hit hard, the mids and highs have been sacrificed.
Vocals are indistinct, and the whole sound is like you're listening through a wet towel.
Really disappointing for the price and build quality.
Great for $10 At this price, it's hard to ask for much more.
It feels a little light and cheap in the hand, but that's understandable.
The sound quality isn't mind blowing, but it's pretty good.

A little tinny and muffled, but perfectly serviceable.

The most disturbing thing for me was a weird mark I found on the edge of my housing.
At closer inspection, I think it's just a defect in the injection moulding, but at first it seemed like some kind of dried bodily fluid from the factory.
It still creeps me out just a bit.
Unique Formfactor, Works Surprisingly Well As a disclaimer, despite looking like a neck pillow, this is certainly not designed to be soft and comforting for a nap.
However, I find this to be an interesting form factor for getting big sound and keeping your hands free.

Earbuds can be fatiguing inside the ears for long periods of time, closed back headphones can be sweaty and fatiguing, open backs are better, but you still have a floppy thing that may or may not clamp onto your head well and can get in the way of you hearing the world.

The tradeoff with these of course is that everyone else can hear what you're listening to, but there's no fatigue wearing these all day at home, doing chores, working at a desk, etc...

The sound quality is- interesting.
Because you essentially have a soundbar strapped to your neck, you get a big wide soundstage that gives you a lot of surround sound depth.
However, you also lose the benefits of earbuds and headphones that seal around the ear and give you stronger bass.
The overall effect is sound that's good, but loses a bit of clarity and depth.

For someone who isn't a serious audiophile, I don't think this would be a big issue at all.

The only other consideration with sound is that of course unlike headphones, the speakers on these won't follow your head.
This means that as you look around, the sound doesn't track with you, so your head kinda turns and floats through the surround sound.
This can take a little while to get used to, and can be distracting at times, but after a while really isn't a big deal at all.

The build quality feels excellent and gives a great vintage/steampunk look with the bright glowing dial.

The dials are smooth, and the setting switch has nice distinctive clicks as you toggle modes.

The sound quality is also surprisingly good.
Past half volume you do get a bit of distortion, but the speaker on this guy is shockingly loud when you try to push it.

At more reasonable volumes it's god a decent sound that's perhaps a little muddy in the lows, but is still totally pleasant for general listening.

As a gift this is an excellent little novelty, because its also perfectly functional as well!

The controls are nice clicky tactile buttons- single presses skip tracks forward and back, whereas holding for a few seconds will adjust the volume up and down.
Simple, but effective.

Sound quality is alright, but muddy.
Highs are decently clear, mids are muffled, and lows have a bit of thump but with very little definition.

Overall effect is it sounds a bit like you have cotton in your ears.

For the price, these aren't the worst, but they wouldn't be my first choice either.

Show vs Nest - I now have both Ok I’m not a highly knowledgeable person when it comes to tech, but I’m not a novice either.
I actually bought the Show 8 and the Google Nest Hub at the same time because they were priced the same.
I figured I would keep the better of the two.
Nest arrived first so I set it up first.
Setup was incredibly easy (I already have a nest mini), eventually easier than the Show.
I also have a gmail account so that speeds up things on the Nest as well.
I wasn’t keeping my photos on Google but it was pretty quick to add favorites in one folder and the Nest is now a digital photo frame.
I have it on my nightstand because when you turn out the lights it really does go dark as well with a hint of the time showing - in full screen size.
I am VERY sensitive to light at night and this doesn’t bother me at all.
I also really like the “good morning” routine that you set up in the Nest better than the Show.

It’s simple enough to ask and get info right before walking out the door.
Once the Show arrived I did the setup thinking it would be easy as I have 3 dots and an Echo already.
So yeah, setup went ok until you explore thinking ALL the reviews are wrong and you CAN turn off the “try this” feature.
The answer is NO, you can’t.
I have every part that should turn it off switched to off (even on the app).
Constant “try this” on the screen.
It’s ALWAYS there.
And there is a list of what seems like a 100 “cards” so it never runs out.
The software must’ve changed because all of the offered suggestions to turn it off aren’t accurate for what is currently possible.

If you don’t care about that/wouldn’t bother you, then choose the unit that dominates your home or the website you use the most.
So which is better?
Meh, they’re about the same IMO.
My sons and I usually have them compete with each other to see which one can answer a question accurately or with the best info.
Lately there’s no clear winner on that, but Google is usually easier to understand.
The Show does NOT go completely dark at night so I could never have it on my nightstand and the clock is never full screen so that’s annoying too.

Neat and tidy solution to save your junk drawer.
When I recently took inventory of my battery stash, I thought there had to be a better way.
As you can see from my photo, I had various types and sizes of packaging all tossed in a kitchen drawer.
It was a mess.
There must be a better way to store these.
And there is.

Apparently, battery cases are a thing.

Of course when I started looking at options, I wanted explosion proof and water resistance.
However after looking at dozens of cases, I realized, where are everyone’s D batteries?
The vast majority of the battery cases had six slots, max, for D batteries.
What?
I have a camping lantern and fan that each take four D batteries.
And what about the 9Vs?
I buy those by the dozen.

When one fire alarm starts chirping, you better have a whole lot of 9Vs.

So I got this case.
I need usability more than I need explosion proofing.

It still doesn’t have enough 9V storage, but I can use extra D and C compartments for those (see photo).

I also wanted one with a pocket for my button batteries.
This has slots, but I’d prefer to keep them packaged as I have various types.
The only reason I deducted 1 Star was because the pocket is not tight, nor does it have a closure.
The handle to carry this case is on the hinge side which becomes the top when carrying the case.
This means that the pocket is upside down when you pick up the case.
In my use, this led to button batteries falling out when I unzipped the case as they had fallen out of the pocket.
It would be great if the pocket held them in.
I solved this but putting all my button batteries inside a large ziplock bag and then inside the pocket.

This way, the tiny packages don’t fall out.

I like this case.
Now my batteries are easily accessible in the pantry.
There is now a ton of free room in my kitchen drawer.

Also, I can easily take stock of what sizes I’m running low on.

Oh and obviously, the tester is a huge bonus.
I have a tornado shelter where I keep cases of batteries for emergencies, not to be used around the house.
It’ll be nice to go test them before each tornado season to see if they’ve outlived their life and need replacing.

Great Once You Remove The Sticky Friction Grease This panoramic camera mount is well made for the price point and my rating would be five stars if it were not for the fact that it is almost unusable until you disassemble the entire product and remove all the friction grease that is covering it.
If you don't, your hands, camera, camera bag, and anything else this product comes in contact with will be covered in sticky goo that simply will not come off with soap and water.
Normally this type of grease would be a good thing, but the grease is not contained within the product, but instead coating parts you will frequently touch.

This means that no matter how careful you are, you will get it everywhere.

I ended up taking everything apart and giving it a good cleaning, removing all of the goo, and making the mount usable.

Here is what I did:

1.

Find the end of both rails that contain a small set screw that prevents the rail from sliding all the way out.
2.

Use a small blade or screwdriver to peel back a little of the rubber pad directly over the set screw enough so you can access it.
3.

Use a 1.5mm hex key to back out the set screw until the rail slides out of the mount.
4.

Use a 3mm hex key to carefully remove the hex bolt that allows the upper rail to pivot.
5.
Take both rails and mounting blocks and spway them with WD-40.

WD-40 acts as a solvent for this type of grease.
6.

Use a toothbrush to clean the teeth on the rails and also the gears in the mounting blocks.
7.

Wipe the excess WD-40 off with a paper towel.
8.

Gently wash the rails and blocks in water and dawn dish soap which will remove the WD-40.
9.

Thoroughly dry the parts.
10.

Reassemble the parts in reverse order.

I ended up using applying some PTFE lubricant which is dry, not sticky and won't attract dirt.

Excellent Entry Level Water Cooling at Reasonable Price This is probably one of the best AIO coolers I have ever installed in a computer system.
I would highly recommend this for anyone looking to get their temps under control.
I am primarily a workstation, coding, multi-VM, type of power user, who happens to play games every once in a while.

Water cooling is not just for gaming and is a powerful component to have for any type of user, so don't let such a simple misconception keep you from enjoying prolonged component life and quieter system operation.

There are a few key things to watch out for though:

1) This matters more for those who will mount the radiator at the front of their case: When measuring your setup to determine whether the rubber hoses are long enough, do not take a linear measurement from the area in your case where the radiator will go over to the CPU.
The rubber hoses are thick and the way they are mounted with a 90 degree elbow at the CPU bracket do not let them lay very flat, they maintain a rather rigid curve to the radiator.
Instead, measure more in a half moon shape from the radiator area over to the CPU.
This will give you a better idea if you are going to have enough length to work with.

If you happen to be mounting this on the rear or top of the case where the radiator is in closer proximity to the CPU, you shouldn't have anything to worry about.

2) When you first turn this on, do not be surprised if there is a lot of noise coming from the motor in the CPU block, including vibrations, gurgling, bubbling, gremlins, gnomes, or other unnatural sounds that may come from it.
During shipping there is no telling how many bubbles have been spread throughout the hoses, radiator, and CPU block.
As long as it sounds like something is moving in there, let it run for several minutes.
It took about 5 minutes before the pump on my system had managed to cycle enough fluid to situate all of the air bubbles where they belong, and the system went dead quiet as soon as it did.
It hasn't made a peep since and has been running silent and flawless for days.
If you are concerned about thermal damage to the processor, remove the RAM from your motherboard so it fails to POST but still maintains power to accessory fans.
This will allow you to clear the system without putting any actual thermal stress on the CPU.

If you're still nervous after the bubbling sounds go away, boot to BIOS and watch your CPU temps from there for a few more minutes to make sure everything looks good.

3) The CPU block comes with some thermal compound already installed and ready to go, which is great if you so happened to forget to buy any before wanting to install this kit.
So right out of the box, this is ready to go which I thought was quite nice but not clearly advertised anywhere.

Now, for those who intend to use this for more high-end processors, heavy gaming, overclocking, etc then I might suggest having an extra plastic scraper handy and scraping this off the copper block so you can cleanly place your own desired thermal cooling paste of choice (Arctic, Deepcool, Grizzly, etc.) on instead.

4) It doesn't take a super nerd or computer genius to install this, though they may be able to complete the process faster.
If you take your time and go slow, just about anyone can do this on their first try without issues.
When in doubt, check out Google or YouTube - there are tons of walk through videos for installing AIO (including this exact one) which cover just about any question you could possibly have.

3-Pack: Pretty pleased so far in 2-Story, 2500 sf house w/stone walls This is our first foray into mesh Wi-Fi and I've got to say we're pretty impressed with this entry-level, three-pack setup.

Fed up with the old wall-plug extenders – both with and without external antennas – we have used with disappointing results over the years, we decided to give this system a go in my mother's 2,500 square foot, two-story house that has partial Austin limestone walls throughout the ground floor.

Working from home, we must have reliable internet everywhere we go and – only a day or so into it – we're pleased so far.

I will say that the signal has ebbed and flowed sometimes but there are so many variables and multiple devices that can make that happen and I've been too preoccupied to experiment with running speed tests and repositioning the cube(s), which are not unattractive.

Perhaps the newer model might yield better results under our circumstances.

This system does require one to use iOS or Android apps for setup, so if you're still using a flip phone (as my 82-year-old mother is) you'll need to find another solution or get a neighbor kid to come help.

The process is no more or less difficult than setting up an Alexa or AirTV device, which could be a bit challenging for some.

Bottom line: now, we can work and satisfactorily stream all over the house so I'm a happy camper, especially given the price point.

I enjoy reading but I also enjoy playing word games which I did on the old version.

REALLY??
Who would make a device purporting to encompass new technology that isn’t backward compatible with older generation programs?
I’m at a loss to understand this logic.
Even Kindle Support wasn’t aware of this non-compatibility - they were also surprised.
I AM HIGHLY DISAPPOINTED!
Lastly, there doesn’t seem to be any word-game programs for the “NEW" generation device.

Mind boggling.

As a reader, it’s very nice.
It’s certainly small and lightweight.
I like the available cover which turns on the device when it’s opened; no more button to push to awaken it.
The backlighting is great compared to my 5th generation Kindle which has a flip-out light built into the case and is powered by the Kindle battery.
The touch screen is very sensitive, almost too sensitive but I’ll get used to it.
The battery life is so-so; certainly not better that my old one....which I expected it to be.
This new device is waterproof - great if I am less careful with it than I am with my phone or if I intend to read under water (lipstick on a pig).
The dictionary function is OK, no better or worse than before, just different in design.
Seems to me like change for the sake if change so it can be said it’s been "improved ".
I have found that the Typo Notification function is better...this I use more than should be required.

Apparently, proof reading is a lost art.

So, all that said, I now have a new "reader" and an old word game device.
To readers of this review: Forewarned is Forearmed.
Just be aware.

Especially when The TV has only one HDMI input and no optical SPDIF output.

And the soundbar has an optical SPDIF input but no HDMI input.

Simply plug the HDMI audio and video source into the avedio HDMI input.
Then, use the HDMI cable (included with avedio) between the avedio HDMI output and the TV HDMI input.

Finally, use an optical cable between the avideo SPDIF output and the soundbar optical SPIF input.

Fine replacement for previous model battery eater My original magic mouse finally went on the fritz - not sure how many years I had it but I liked having a wireless mouse.
I had also gotten used to the feel of the mouse, the gestured needed to switch screens, right and left click and so on.
What I never got used to was the battery usage.
It seemed every other week or so, I would get the screen notification that the mouse batteries were low and need to be changed soon.
I keep my used batteries in a bag so that I can take them to recycling.

I have a large bag full of batteries, many or which were used in the mouse.

The other problems with the original mouse were also battery-related: the door that enclosed the batteries was hard to fasten tightly with the result that it would fall off from time to time when I moved the mouse.

The batteries also had to be snugly fit and if there was any looseness, which did happen from time to time, the mouse would lose blue-tooth connectivity periodically, connecting and reconnecting repeatedly.

It took awhile for me to figure out this was a battery issue.

Still, I liked the mouse in spite of these annoyances and maybe I'm just a bit set in my ways.
When the mouse finally died and no amount of jiggering could sustain the blue tooth connection and the battery compartment door just would not stay on, it was finally time.

That is when I bought the Magic Mouse 2, a few weeks ago.

I am beyond happy with it.
All of the battery-related problems have been eliminated.
No more frequent changes, no more fiddling with the battery compartment door or batteries themselves.
This mouse just works and I have had none of the other problems that other reviewers have reported.
I don't find it uncomfortable, it's responsiveness is fine, and I don't have blue tooth connectivity problems.

Every other night or so when I turn off my monitor, I hook the mouse up to its charger, which is connected to a USB hub, and I'm ready to go in the AM.

I would say that if you are a current or former magic mouse user looking to upgrade and get rid of the battery-eating model, this is a good choice for you.
You will maintain continuity with the mouse gestures you've grown used to using and the feel of the mouse will be identical.

I also recommend getting a Logitech wireless solar keyboard to free yourself from the cord completely while also not needing batteries or even recharging.

If, however, you are used to other mouse types with a larger body and defined keys for left and right clicking, you might find this mouse a bit uncomfortable and foreign and should look elsewhere.

Finally a Kindle that I can keep for long term I have owned a few different generations of Kindles in the past and have generally loved reading on them.

I like the fact that it gives you great convenience of holding tons of books wherever you go in a very compact form factor, and the impressive battery life thanks to the e-paper technology.

The last Kindle I had was a 9th generation Oasis, which was an upgrade from a Paperwhite.
I was very much disappointed with the 9th generation Oasis mainly due to issues with the screen backlight.
The backlight on the device had uneven light distribution on the screen - so one side of the screen (where the buttons are placed) was very brightly lit when compared to the other side.
And the issue was something which cannot be ignored since it was quite evident while reading in dark when you have to completely rely on the backlight to see the text.
It was a bad experience for me since I had to pay a premium price for an ebook reader.

I had got it replaced twice but the issue still persisted, indicating that the design of the product itself had the issue.

While I was struggling with the 9th generation Oasis, I saw that the 10th generation was out and apparently the backlight issues were no longer present in the new device.
I waited for some time for the reviews to flow in to see if there were any major issues with it.

And finally, I traded in my 9th generation Oasis with the 10th generation and I am so glad that I made the decision to upgrade to 10th generation.

All my complaints from the previous generations are solved, and the amber lighting on the screen is amazing and I now use it almost 100% of the time.
It gives you the feeling like you are reading on a real paper book.
The 300 ppi resolution of the screen is very crisp for daily reading and the battery life is good enough but it could have been better.

I feel that this is a Kindle that I can finally keep for a longer time to read my books and I am happy that Amazon made this small incremental update to fix an issue they had with the previous generation.
I would have appreciated even more if they had acknowledged the screen issue they had but anyway, I am happy with this upgrade.
Worth upgrading!

The scroll wheel matches the underside.

The blue mouse looks good when used with a navy blue or royal blue laptop (like the ASUS Zenbook UX370).

This mouse is smaller than a normal desktop mouse, but not as tiny as some travel mice.
Will fit most hands comfortably.

I'm 6'2" with large hands and enjoy using the mouse when sitting at the couch, while my 5'1" daughter with small hands can use the mouse anywhere for many hours doing school work without issue.

The mouse has a small blue light that flashes when in Bluetooth pairing mode.

Ordered this mouse from Amazon, received the next day, pulled the mouse from its package, opened the battery door and removed the pull-tape from the battery, closed the battery door, and while the blue light was flashing on the mouse, turned on a Bluetooth-equipped Windows laptop, went into the Control Panel, Devices, Bluetooth, Add Device, and Windows immediately paired with the mouse.
No special software install necessary for Windows 10.
Easy setup!

Logitech states this mouse will work with Mac and Windows computers, Android mobile devices and Chromebooks.

The mouse has an on/off switch adjacent to the battery door.
It was "on" when received new, but there is a pull-tape for shipping to avoid the mouse running until you unpack it.
I believe the mouse automatically sleeps when not in use, but this doesn't present a challenge to wake-up when you're ready to use again.

The small blue light on the mouse only flashes when in pairing mode, and doesn't appear to turn on at any other time, effectively hidden.

The optic under this mouse works on many different surface types without issue, to include wood tables, white plastic tables, leather armrests, cloth armrests, blue plastic and gray plastic surfaces of laptop palmrests, jeans, etc.
I haven't tested this mouse on a clear glass table, which may give it a challenge.

If you absolutely need a mouse that will work on _any_ surface, the "Logitech MX Anywhere 2S" model uses darkfield technology which reportedly will work on clear glass (and costs significantly more than this M535 model).

When shipped, the mouse will arrive in clear plastic packaging.

The backside of the plastic is perforated, making it very easy to open, _without_ having to cut into the plastic with scissors or other tools.

The primary benefit of using a Bluetooth mouse versus a wireless USB mouse is that operating in native Bluetooth mode with a PC or Android device that supports Bluetooth allows you to use the mouse without having to deal with a small USB dongle necessary in other wireless models.

This is an especially important feature for newer model thin laptops that don't have many USB ports, and/or you may not want an extruding dongle connected to the laptop.

In daily operation, I've not encountered any challenges with this mouse.
Works well in Windows 10 with default settings.
No problems with accuracy, lag or jitter.

Responds well during light gaming sessions.

Overall, thumbs up, and would buy again!
No complaints.

After using this for about a week, this is my impression:
- The battery doesn't last very long after kid is separated from caretakers.
We were at Grandma's,  and kids, with my permission, left with their aunts for an hour or 2.

By the time they returned, their batteries were down to 20% or so, and the devices ran out of juice pretty soon after. 2 hours are hopefully enough to find a missing kid, but you can't send kid with a caretaker who doesn't have the app installed, without risking battery drain.
- The devices are waterproof, and by that, I mean, laundry proof.

A device got accidentally left on an outfit my kid discarded, and survived the entire wash routine with no trouble.
- The many ways to attach the device to kids are all useful.
My 2 year old, I need to use the pin pouch to attach it to her, otherwise, she will manage to get rid of it, somehow.

My older 2, one prefers it in his pocket, and the other prefers it on a belt clip hidden under his shirt.
- They work well, overseas.
- You can't talk to kids through them, or hear the kids.
- They can be very frustrating in apartment buildings or malls, where you can see that the kid is somewhere in the gigantic building, but not where.
- You can make the jiobit ring, which is useful for finding it, but also for letting kids know that they need to turn up.

Overall, these are very lightweight, and the only usable trackers in the market, but could still do with substantial improvement!

I have installed this product on a Nintendo Switch, two iPads, and an iPhone.

Actually, I have installed it three times on the same iPhone because the screen protector broke on two separate occasions when I dropped it, the first time on a mountain trail, and the second time on asphalt.
The screen protector, although it cracked, protected my screen on both occasions.
For those who are concerned about bubbles, I suggest that you carefully read every instruction before beginning your installation.
Then get yourself situated with everything you need.
Put all the supplies on the table in front of you as if you were about to perform surgery.
Choose an area with good lighting, and no dust.
Minimize dust potential by turning off fans or closing windows.
Consider removing sweaters or other articles of clothing that could drop lint in your workspace.
Finally, wash your hands and don’t hesitate to let them air dry.
When you are ready to begin your installation, read the instructions again.

If after all of these efforts you spot a piece of dust under the shield, gently life the protector by the corner closest to the speck, and use the edge of a plastic spoon to gently scrape the speck of dust toward the edge until it can fall away.
Do not touch the underside of the shield with your fingers.
Once the speck is removed, let the corner make contact with the screen again and smooth out any bubbles.
The protector should be invisible if it is installed correctly.
I hope this helps.
Good luck!

Well the only credit I will give the developer is that they finally delivered on functionality at a mediocre level.

Reliability is still lurking somewhere between the bottom of the dumpster and the oily, grimy asphalt below it.

The good:
-The cameras (we use 2 orbs as baby monitor cams, WARNING: these rarely stay on longer than 30 minutes, so it's not a set it and fall asleep camera) have great night vision, like super detailed night vision
-The resolution/quality is a 8/10 (they offer UltraHD, HD, and Standard in the app settings, but it's not truly UltraHD.

Probably 1080p I think)
-The mics are super sensitive so you can hear baby's softest whimpers or cries.

The bad (I'll abridge this list for the sake of time):
-Alexa compatibility is awful.
If you can get it to work on FireTV sticks and/or FireTV Cube (we have both), it's decent.
There's a timeout (not sure if it's intentional or a software flaw as it's never a set amount of time) where it just closes the camera after 10-35 minutes.

This also happens on the iPhone app (I'll talk about that in a second), but at least does you the service of warning you with a 15-20 second countdown so you can push to keep it going.
-The FireTV app does not offer ANY interactive features.
You can only tell the Alexa to show the camera by name.
You also cannot just switch to another camera with your voice.
It will freeze the app.

You must go home, wait 5-10 seconds, then tell it to show a different camera.
-The iPhone app (also on the iPad as a shrunken iPhone version) is decent, like 6/10 decent.

It has been updated over a dozen times since we started and it now offers what you'd expect in 2020: split screen for multi-camera view (not available on FireTV apps, just mobile/tablets), various settings, controls to move your camera around the room, FaceID/TouchID, etc.
The auto-record motion detection is garbage, fills up your cloud, and the cloud itself is the most confusing thing in the world to setup.

You get a free month trial but if you try to stop it/extend it, etc it just doesn't confirm you've done anything and always says it's active
-The Alexa Skill is pure garbage, with limited functionality and hit or miss everytime you try to login.
I'm actually writing this review right now because for the umpteenth time the skill has stopped working on my FireTV Cube and I tried the usual disable, re-enable and re-login.

Usually works but now the site to login just won't load, via the app or the web browser.

Good luck if you already bought into this company and are stuck.
If you're considering it, DON'T!!
Spend the money and get something more reliable.

Great outdoor camera for the money Overall, this camera is great for the money and does exactly what is advertised.
I'm glad I waited for a month to write a review because some of the areas that I felt were lacking turned out to be supported.
The camera setup was easy for me.

It quickly connected to my wifi and began to work.

The Netvue app is good too.
It shows live feeds and stores still shots of any motion detected.
At first, I couldn't figure out how to replay the video for the still shots but I figured it out.

It is actually very cool because it appears that the camera is always recording to the local memory card so you can easily go back to the point in time that the motion was detected and play the video before/after.
That was something that I had to figure out but has been working flawlessly ever since.
I highly recommend buying the max memory card with the unit.

You won't need to use Cloud storage if you have sufficient storage in the camera.

One of the best features is the ability to interface with Alexa.
We have a Fire TV and I can simply say "Alexa, show the front door" and I will immediately see the live feed on my TV.
That is so cool!!

There are a few minor complaints that I have but they really are minimal compared to the great features:
-There are three cords that come out of the back of the camera.
Not a big deal if you plan to mount on a wall and tuck the cords behind it.
However, if you mount direct to a surface like I did, the cords will hang out.
I had to wrap them in a plastic bag and rubber band them to the top of the camera.

It doesn't look pretty but it works.
-The motion detection isn't perfect.
Most of the alerts come from headlights as cars go by.

There were a few times that it didn't catch a package delivery but the majority of the time, I get an instant notification when cars are going up and down the driveway.
-The live playback is a little choppy but still very good.

Again, this camera is definitely worth it for the money.
The features will definitely outweigh any minor inconveniences.

I ended up grinding down and smoothing the metal interface on my sliding window, then using "coax rubber" (the type you use to seal coax fittings outside) on the metal ridge to "soften" the transition.

Nothin' Defeats SoundPEATS This is my first pair of truly wireless earbuds.
Other devices I have include a Plantronics Voyager Focus, which is my primary go-to at work, Powerbeats 3, and a pair of soundpeats magnetic bluetooth workout earbuds (similar to Powerbeats).
These TrueCapsules are my favorite, hands-down.

(The Powerbeats are my least favorite)

Pros:
While the Focus is pretty tough to beat in terms of battery life and noise cancellation (for both mic and speakers), the TrueCapsules are the most comfortable buds I've ever owned.
I'm usually not a fan of ear buds.
I have an oddly shaped right ear canal, and because of that I can never seem to find a earbud diaphragm that works properly.
Especially when working out, they always tend to wiggle loose and fall out.
Historically, the only earbuds that have stayed put for me have been the standard Apple earphones, which don't really "suction" into place, but simply rest in your ear.
Until now!
SoundPeats nailed it; their diaphragm is the perfect size and texture for my weird ear.
They are very comfortable for me, unlike my Powerbeats, which start hurting my ears after a half-hour or so (and doesn't sit properly in my right ear, anyways).

And they fit better.

I am not an audiophile.
I listen to a lot of music and I have my own ideas of when music sounds good and when it sounds lousy.
These earbuds, in my opinion, outperform my Powerbeats, in regard to audio quality.
Hard to believe the Soundpeats device is going to produce better audio than Beats hardware, but they sound better, to me.
If I had to guess why, I'd say it's because they sit more flush in my ear, which lets me hear a wider range of sound and deeper bass.

I don't think the battery life is quite as good as the Powerbeats, but I'm still VERY happy with this purchase.

Cons:
I'm still trying to get used to the touch controls; I think you can do everything you might need to do with different variations of tap and touch, but I try to keep the manual nearby.
I'm also always accidentally pausing music and turning them on when I don't want to.

Turning the volume up/down is a pretty slow endeavor, but these are minor gripes that shouldn't dissuade anyone from trying these guys out.

UPDATE - Three Years Later
My beloved SoundPEATS earbuds fell apart recently when I was trying to find a more optimal-fitting ear cushion.
The glue holding the two plastic pieces together gave way and ... bam. i could see the innards of the left earbud.
Immediately I thought to myself: well, i can either try to get creative with a little superglue, or I could drop $150 bones on a higher quality set of buds.
Superglue did the trick.
We're back in business.

Great sound but be prepared for a learning curve on how to command your Echo!
Received my echo 3rd Gen unit over the holidays due to an ongoing promotion.
It has great sound over the Dot version hands down - good base and highs.
It takes a bit of investment of your time to learn all the nuances of what Alexa can do for you.

With the app, you can set up your Echo to be an alarm clock, timer, grocery list, teach it a routine for each day (like giving the weather forecast, the latest news from a specific news source, turn on/turn off lights, thermostat control, play specific music (classical, rock, pop) etc.).
But beware, the instructions for all this are not included with your Echo.
You have to dig around (through e-books, YouTube, etc.) to become familiar with the commands and required outcomes.
For example, my unit began to display a pulsating yellow light that became annoying at night in my bedroom.
I couldn’t turn it off except by disconnecting the power.
Of course, this could’ve become a deal breaker if I had to disconnect every nite (I kept all the shipping package just in case I needed to return it).
Well, it turned out that this was one way the Echo communicates with you.
It was trying to tell me It had a notification for me to listen to.
Until I asked, “Alexa, do I have any notification?”
the yellow pulsating light would’ve continued.
Immediately after delivering all notifications, the yellow pulsating light stopped.
By the way, the notifications were about shipping/delivery of packages coming from, wait for it...
Amazon.
Of course, other types of notifications are possible pending how you program your Echo.
Like I said, this simple issue would’ve been a deal breaker for me if I hadn’t decided to invest some of my time in trying to resolve this simple problem.
It wasn’t until I learned how to communicate with my Echo that the problem wouldn’t go away.
But again, the answer was not included with this product.
My feedback to Amazon would be to include a list of commands and a trouble shooting section for the buyer.
By employing this one simple act, I’m sure these products would be in far more demand by their customers once they learn the how to’s of communicating with these aliens.

I'm impressed with the video once it's got a good signal I selected this system out of a dozen based on what its attributes were and a good price.

This is my first venture into this kind of system and the learning curve was pretty steep for this old man.

My application was to monitor the carport parking area in a detached carport 30' wide that has 3 enclosed storage areas 4' deep that the tenants in a two story triplex use.
It is 30' from the triplex and a wired system was not an option unless some major work was done.

Both the triplex and carport have aluminum siding so I knew that might be an issue.

When I ordered it I also ordered some power extension cords and two power splitter setups, plus a large hard drive.
Upon arrival I formatted the hard drive and assembled the system inside on the ground level to test the camera's using a TV for a display screen.
I then moved the cameras outside and things looked good.
The next test was to place the camera's under the planed position on each end of the carport and the signals were blocked by three walls and lots of storage items.

Placing the camera's outside the carport didn't help because the Network Video Recorder (NVR) was positioned roughly in the middle of the carport under the TV so the position change did nothing.

Next I moved the NVR upstairs and on a wall that was about inline with one end of the carport.
Once again I positioned the camera's on the ground on both ends of the carport and had only one show up on an old computer monitor.

Because camera's were on ground level the items in the storage area were suspect as well as walls.

I decided to install two cameras In the carports wooden ceiling where I planned they would go which should eliminate the storage area's items and possibly one wall given the angle.

This helped but signal strength was weak so I contacted the support team via email and explained my situation.

This support team has vastly different working hours than I do so answers to a question often took a day to get to me but these guys were willing to help and kept in contact.
Frankly, if they weren't for them I might have gave up.
They ended up sending me a signal booster (IPC Router) and this was the start of a steep learning curve for me.
The booster manual (quick guide) needs to be read 'carefully' so not to miss details and the pictures were not so clear to me so I missed some important points.
This is where the support guys really helped.
My first impression of how this booster worked was wrong and after many attempts to get it right, I finally got it.

All four cameras now show good videos on screen and the the time stamps in each is within a couple seconds of each other.

If you have a line of sight that is not hindered much this system should meet ones needs and the time stamp should be close to each of the other in a multi-camera setup.
If line of sight has interference of one kind or another, you may see larger variances in the time stamp if they show up at all.
In that situatin you may need a booster to improve the signal.

Should you go that route be sure to read the manual "carefully" and "completely" and don't be afraid to ask the support team for help.

The support team is there to help and I appreciate how they helped me.

Pros: I've owned the LG Tone Ultra series beginning with the HBS-810, HBS-820s, and now these.
The size of this LG Tone series is preferable for me.
Flexible, not clunky and stiff, and I typically don't feel neck fatigue because of its humble footprint.
Also, I carry 2 phones, so the multipoint feature is welcome.
Overall, the performance in audio and voice quality has improved tremendously.

Older models didn't perform as well in voice quality during voice calls -- many clients of mine were complaining of background noise or spotty voice quality -- it didn't make for a good professional Bluetooth headset.
I struggled to use the older models during my work day, which translated to less reasons to use them altogether.
But with this new series, I hope was delivered.

Improved Bluetooth 5.0 technology along with dual mems, quad layer speaker technology delivers both great balanced audio sound with good level of highs and bass, while allowing me to take much clearer voice calls.
Multipoint connection is great for someone like me who carries 2 phones simultaneously able to connect this headset to both phones.
The LG smartphone app helps me control these headsets from either phones, added features, control and monitoring.
Lastly, the best feature of these headsets is the voice feedback, but also the haptic feedback.
The haptic feedback is the best feature of these headsets and unique to it from any other Bluetooth headsets I've owned.
If I get a call, I like that it vibrates around my neck.
I love that.
Also, battery life is exceptional.

They last me 2 days if needed.
Cons: Only a few but they are quite disruptive to my ability to really enjoy them.
First, I must say the Bluetooth connectivity is spotty.
It doesn't automatically connect to my devices.
With the updated Bluetooth 5.0 connectivity, I had hoped for a much smoother flawless experience, but it just doesn't deliver.
I find myself having to search and connect to these headsets many times manually.
I had other multipoint headsets that automatically connect to both phones simultaneously, which spoiled me.
I had hoped that these LG HBS-835s series would do just that.
Instead, I feel like the Bluetooth connectivity is a step down even from the LG HBS820s.
Secondly, maybe it's the one I received, but the power plug in seems a bit jenki.
I have to jiggle it a little in order to make sure the microUSB connection is getting power therefore properly charging the unit.

Lastly, that's just it, I said microUSB -- by now, I was hoping we would already be on USB-c.
Summary: The HBS-835s almost delivers on a near perfect richly featured headset experience.
It does deliver on the items that count, voice and audio quality.

But the lack of reliable and consistent Bluetooth connectivity draws it down, and unfortunately disrupts the overall experience enough, considering Bluetooth 5.0 technology promises that didn't deliver.
So close and yet so far away -- hoping that an update in firmware can solve these simply issues.

Terrific Motherboard for Ryzen 7 3800X and GSkill 3600 Memory I purchased this Motherboard during the Black Friday sales, and received an incredible deal.

(Thank You Amazon.).

I am using this with a Ryzen 7 3800X and 16 Gb of GSkill "Neo" RAM at 3600 speed, 16-19-19 timings.
To be clear, I had absolutely NO issues with this Motherboard.
Mine was not set up with the latest BIOS, so I used the BIOS flashback to be able to run the most up to date BIOS in support of Ryzen 3000.
Worked like a charm.

I am getting peak CPU speeds of over 4500, and everything is working great.

A couple of caveats that I did discover: 1.
The Ryzen 7 3800X idles hot, (47 Degrees C.), and at 1.47 Volts on auto settings.

It is actually fine there, and in stress testing with AIDA 64, I did not go over 72 Degrees C.
Also, if you want to use the X4 direct PCIe 3.0 lanes direct to the CPU for NVME storage, use the BOTTOM M.2 slot, and not the top one by the CPU Socket.

Using the top one by the CPU socket will cut your PCIe slot 1, (Main Graphics Card) to a 8X lane bandwidth rather than the 16X bandwidth.
So far, ASUS has issued 2 BIOS updates for the Crosshair VII in support of Ryzen 3000, so ASUS is continuing to support this Platform.

From all the things I have been reading about the X570 Motherboards, I am kind of glad to be on X470 for now.

Also know that you will not get peak performance out of the Ryzen 3800X CPU with the Wraith Prism cooler.

It will be functional, and be fine, but you will get better performance out of a more robust cooler, whether air or water.

Not sure what else to add.
Everything that was supposed to be in the box, was in the box.

First impressions: Solid, well made, heavier than expected, clear display with smart or switchable backlight, smooth controls, stainless steel telescoping antenna - not plated brass, very nice padded case, charging cord, ear buds, wire antenna, single removable Li-Ion 18650 cell that charges in radio, good English user manual, high fidelity speaker.

It is easy to delete memories with one key press.

It has a "kickstand" on the back so you can lay it down at an angle without as much risk of tipping it over.
It has rubber feet on the bottom.
It has a "line out" jack.
It has a clock with alarm function and sleep timer.
The tuning and volume knobs are very smooth and solid with a viscous sort of resistance.
Not sloppy or lose.

The display shows signal strength in DB and signal to noise ratio in DB.

It is sensitive.
I picked up a couple of 40 meters LSB QSOs using only the telescoping antenna.
I picked up several SW stations using only the telescoping antenna.
My location is not good for broadcast FM but I picked up several of those as well.
One complaint is that the audio is quite bass heavy even though there is a tone switch on the side.

If you are within range of a good FM station it will sound much bigger than it's small size.
