nearly perfect - sturdy, great price, but had to figure out install i've had these cord clips up and running for a couple months now and they have been great once installed:

i have them installed to clip an ethernet cable that's basically running through my entire house. they are sturdy enough that if someone accidentally hits them, they do not budge. however, if you need to take them out, it's as simple as just pulling/twisting them off the surface with your fingers - won't hurt your wrist and hasn't done any damage to the paint or wooden floors that i've pried them out of (your mileage may vary though depending on what surface you're using).

they can be clip cables both from the left and from the right, so they're pretty versatile as well. i have them running all sorts of shapes across the edges of my floor.

OK!
so why the minus one star?

installation...specifically installing with tape instead of screws. i figured out a good way to do this so don't worry, but it took some trial and error. let me explain:

the package gives you a bunch of double-sided tape if you want to install this via tape as opposed to screws. the tape itself is clear colored but the covers on both sides are read. it's really really hard to peel off one side of the tape cover. like i destroyed several of these double-sided tapes in an effort to peel the cover off the second side of the tape. what i eventually started doing is as follows:

1) peel the tape cover off the side of the tape that's easy to peel, and stick that peeled side onto the cord clip.
2) take a knife and cut that tape (the one already taped to the cord clip) in half. now, the tape is already stuck to the cord clip so the tape isn't going anywhere. the plastic of the cord clip is sturdy so it should be easy to cut just the tape and not the the cord clip.
3) use the knife (or your fingers) to find the newly formed edge(s) that you just made on the tape cover by cutting it, and peel the second side of the tape cover from there.

it wasn't so bad after i discovered this... but it would have been nice if i didn't have to cut the tape cover for every clip installed.

works after you straighten it out via boiling water verifying what another reviewer wrote about putting this product into boiling (not just warm) water.

so why am i so happy?
the ui (user interface) on this box is much improved over previous models. in fact, it's a damn joy!

while i am not an audiophile, i can tell u, it really delivers. it has about 10% less power than my rx-a1000 but it's not even noticeable when cranked.

many folks are interested in atmos and 9.1 (presence spkrs). well, i can tell u, my very antiquated 5.1 and 7.1 sets, put out and it's unlikely that i'll do anything more than 5.1 in the future. i judge the audio in this manner:
1) movies: the dark knight and avatar 3d
2) antenna/live and streamed tv.
4) audio (music) from a local (home) server
that said (written), all my yammies perform quite well. the rx-a1000 is king when cranked and the entire 3200sq ft 2 floor house shakes with only one 15" subwoofer at < 50%. this rx-a780 is also impressive even with less power and smaller speakers - again, the entire house shakes (12" sub) but the highs are crisp and the sub is not in a corner.

so yes, very happy. you may ask, why not 5 stars?

You need to create a 2TB partition (or less) and have the remaining partitions within reach of the 2TB for backward compatibility with the Master Boot Record (MBR).
The specs should have included a information on how to create minimal legacy bootstrap-partitions at the beginning of the disk where the MBR could easily point.

This would be "dummy" partitions whose purpose is nothing except to contain a bootmgr, which would in turn point into the actual full size of the remaining  ( > 2TB ) partitions and HDD.There is no easy BIOS fix.
I ended up returning to my 2TB HDD and used this larger drive as a storage HDD with GPT format.
I moved iCloud and DropBox links there too to start saving actual primary HDD space with 2TB on it.
You might be better getting an external USB drive or again just use this drive for additional storage with the GPT formatting.

Just a little bit of a learning curve Well before computers existed, I learned to type on a typewriter.
Years later,I was using tower computers with full sized mechanical keyboards.
The last few years it has been laptops with the more compact keyboards.
I've never gotten used to the compact keyboard of a laptop, (nice when traveling, but a pain at home), so I finally decided to go full sized and I selected this one.
Good choice!
I love just the fact that it is full sized.
With the included built in trackball, this thing is a monster compared to my laptop keyboard.
Good!
On the laptop my old arthritic fingers were always tapping wrong keys causing me to cuss and swear in frustration.
I find and press the keys on this keyboard with ease and I love the long travel mechanical feel.
No guesswork whether I've pressed a key.

I can again type without constantly glancing down at the keyboard.

I am often on the computer at night so the back lit keyboard is a definite plus.
Press Fn and the number 8 key to turn on the light.
A second time makes it brighter.
A third time makes the light irritatingly fade in and out.
(I won't be using that fade in and out feature.)
If you have reached the fade in and out mode and press Fn and the number 2 key, the fading stops and the keyboard is one step BRIGHTER.
After that, multiple presses of Fn and 2 dim and eventually turn the light off.
Learning to type on a full sized mechanical keyboard  again is taking some getting used to after the laptops keyboard, but I know it will not take long to become second nature.
With my laptop keyboard I accidentally pressed the num lock key about a million times when intending to press the backspace key to correct a typing error.
Then I press the delete key and get a period.
Now I have to backspace, hit the num lock key and hit the delete key.
All just to correct one miss-typed letter.
That's doesn't happen with this keyboard.
Note that because this is mechanical that there is a lot of clacking noise while you are typing.
I like the feel and the sound, but no doubt it will drive anyone else in the room crazy.
Not my problem.

It's my house.

The trackball has a slightly bigger learning curve for me as I was used to using a wireless ergonomic trackball.
But with that thing my twitchy fingers were always unintentionally pressing the buttons.
That doesn't happen here because my fingers don't rest on the buttons.
Having those buttons below the ball rather than above it takes some getting used to, but it seems to work for me.
The scroll wheel works fine for me too and includes the press button function.
If you're used to a scroll button that you can push left and right as well then you're out of luck here.
My other trackball didn't do that so I don't miss the function.
I've experienced more learning curve by having to maneuver this trackball with my fingers rather than my thumb.
Not a problem.
Just different.
I did have to go in and adjust my mouse settings as once I hooked this keyboard and trackball up, the mouse cursor was moving a hundred miles per hour.
It was slower on my previous trackball.
I just slowed the cursor down and I increased the number of lines the scroll wheel would scroll up or down as scrolling was kind of slow.
That was all I needed to change.
I've had no issues with the trackball not cooperating and have been able to float my cursor all around the screen with no issues.
There is a review that points out an issue with the trackball, but I've had no such problem.
That review is over three years old so maybe there has been a design improvement since then.
I don't know, but it works fine for me.
Something I didn't see in the listing for this keyboard is that the trackball glows when you use it.
It's light is off when you aren't using it, but as soon as you start to roll it around it glows like a dimly smoldering coal.
Pretty cool!
I just got and installed this keyboard, but am so far very satisfied.
If I were to complain about anything it would be that the space bar is kind of small.
It's actually slightly smaller than the space bar on my laptop.
This is due to that 'menu' key to the right of it.
No worries though.

It works fine for me, I haven't had any issues hitting it and I think I like that 'menu' key and will be using it.

The only other thing I might wish for is that the keyboard would have some USB ports.
My laptop has two ports.
My laptop sits on a cooler which plugs into one of those USB ports.
The cooler has two USB ports but one is used to connect it to the laptop.
That leaves me with two USB ports.
One on the laptop and one on the cooler.
This keyboard/trackball used those two USB ports so I have none left.

I'll have to purchase a USB hub to get more ports to use for external drives, USB sticks and charging things.

As stated above, this keyboard connects to two of your computers USB ports.
A nice design feature is that there is only one cable coming out of the keyboard.
Near the end it splits into two short pieces each with it's own USB plug.

Nice to not have two different cables snaking around getting tangled.

So, other than a slightly small space bar and no USB ports, this keyboard is perfect for me.

On more update:
I did have an issue with the trackball not functioning after my laptop resumed from hibernation mode.
I solved this by going into device settings and changing power settings for USB root hub.
I unchecked the box that allowed the computer to turn it off to save power.
Problem solved.
The keyboard did not suffer this issue as the power option was already unchecked for that port.

If you aren't from my area I suggest you try your zip code here and see what it recommends.

I live in Bucks County PA outside of Philadelphia.
I was only interested in getting the main local channels from the antenna (3,6,10,17,29,57 - ABC/NBC/CBS/FOX/etc) but this antenna was actually able to find 33 channels for me!
I even tested it on my basement TV thinking this would be the hardest place to find a signal.
I'm not sure what all the other ones are but it is definitely working.

I've only been using it for a few days so far but the picture quality for HD is really good too, doesn't look much visibly different than picture from a Fios box.

The only obvious tip to give is to read the instructions with the antenna.
Simply plugging in the antenna and going to channel doesn't work.
I tried this first and got nervous when nothing was found.
The instructions indicate that you must connect the antenna and run a channel scan from the TV in order to find the channels.

After doing this, the 33 channels were found.

As for this model itself, it is very small and light.
The flat panel antenna is paper thin, literally, to the point where I questioned if there was actually anything in there.
It comes with one side black and other white to give options for color match on a wall mount.
The antenna connects to the TV thru a provided coax cable, about 8-10 feet I'd estimate.
The amplifier connects to the antenna thru coax cable (provided) and is also pretty small, about the size of a travel tissue package.
The amplifier needs a power connection which is provided for plug in to outlet or you can connect to a USB port on the TV for power which is what I did and works well.
The amplifier and all provided coax in my set were white.

The receiver is pretty “thin” sounding once the volume goes up.

Despite the relatively modest 140wpc on this amp, it brings back the power in spades.

Compared to more expensive Rotel amps, I find the Marantz to be more full, warm, and musical, perhaps at the slight loss of detailed transparency.

The amp doesn’t really stand up to the likes of McIntosh, where the 456 or 9000 far richer detail and musicality.

With the McIntosh you can feel every vibration of a string, where as with the Marantz you hear beautiful music.

So there it is, this is a great little amp that hangs with competitors 2-3x the price, but very rightfully so doesn’t hang with competitors 10x the price.

I think on anything less than B&W 800 series level speakers, this Marantz amp would have you very well covered.

Just what I was looking for, but beware of the battery life I decided on the 13.5 Surface Book 2 with built in NVidia card for several reasons.

I needed something that I could take hand-written notes on for work, and I also wanted something that I could do some light gaming on from the couch.
As for handwriting, this really is a great tool when paired with the Surface Pen.

I am able to rapidly take handwritten notes and share across devices, insert pdfs to quickly fill out or take notes on, and the fact that it separates into a separate tablet means that if I need more mobility, or want to do a little drawing, I have that option as well.

Compared to my girlfriend's new iPad, I think that it is on par, or juuuust a tiny smidge short of the precision level, but as a cursive writer, I wanted something ultra precise and this device certainly is.
It also does a great job running the types of games I like in my leisure time.
The tall aspect ratio means I get more screen than with my old 13.5 inch Asus Zenbook.
It has not issue running RTS and TBS games like Total War, Panzer IV, or Civ VI.
Even more graphics heavy games like Tropico 6 run very smoothly at the 3000x2000 resolution.
HOWEVER, I had to tinker with the battery settings quite a bit to get good life when doing heavy gaming.

I basically had to set the battery settings, even when plugged in, to "best battery life" (as opposed to "best performance"), and you also want to make sure that the game is running on the NVidia graphics card, and not the on-board intel.

One thing that is both a benefit and a hindrance to this device, is that there are two graphics "cards" in the NVidia version I purchased: the NVidia card and battery in the screen half, and the Intel parts and battery in the keyboard half.

The computer defaults to running down the battery in the screen first, which means that when I am gaming I am getting 2-2.5 hours battery life before the screen batter falls below 5% and it crashes the game.
This isn't a HUGE deal, as I dont get as many opportunities to play that long without interruption, but I thought it might be helpful to some others considering this device.

I can say that it charges very fast, and even a short break of 30 minutes can get me to at least a third, almost half battery.
I only have two other complaints about this device: first, the power cord seems really flimsy to me.
It connects on the RH side with a magnet, and can connect both ways, but it falls out ALOT when I am sitting with this in my lap.
More annoying than anything, except the cord is having a tendency to kink at the connection, and it has gotten VERY hot once or twice.
Not sure if this is a regular product issue, or if this is because I purchased a refurbished item.
Speaking of refurbished, my volume button is a little wonky - the volume up side rests lower than the volume down side.
Again, not sure if this is a regular product issue or a refurbished issue, but I am guessing the latter because the aesthetics of it drives me crazy.

Buuuuut, not a big enough complaint to raise a stink over, just my OCD going off.
I definitely am loving this device.
The handwriting part alone has eliminated a hundred legal pads and sticky notes in my office, and syncing OneNote to my phone means that I have my notes anywhere I go.
Would entirely recommend.

SONY finally came up with something I like (review for Sony X10 headphones in silver) I'm in an apartment that I need to move out of soon, and I do almost all of my listening these days with
headphones in any case.

If I find headphones fatiguing, I never listen to them: they end up gathering dust.
Or, if I find their overall performance crap, or the sound dull.

Goodbye.

Having said that, I'm not really a huge fan of Sony's headphones these days.

I do own a 2008 Sony
home theater in a box set, which is decent but not outstanding (not top end), and a small Sony 2011
bookshelf system with Ipod dock--which sounds good for basic apt. background listening and radio),
so I do own some basic Sony audio stuff which is good for certain things.

I feel like their headphones
are hit or miss though lately, with quality, build, and performance.

I don't really love Bluetooth because I like
being able to control the ampage and EQ as much as possible with wired setups, and the still-iffy quality of
wireless audio.

I wanted cans that offer much better bass response than most of the other quite excellent headphones I've bought the past five years or so.
Some have tons of bass, like Koss PortaPros or the wonderful Linsoul Pro ZS10 IEMs.

The PortaPros are great but a bit flimsy
and delicate, though totally portable, and the IEMs are great when I want the IEM sound and portability,
but sometimes I don't want to feel isolated as IEMs can sometimes make you feel like.

I also recently invested in a pair of Audio-Technica MH20xs, good budget studio monitor cans, but, they aren't really super bass-cannons, and they are a bit analytical and "dry," and this is not what I want from a pair of totally "fun", warm, bass-heavy headphones for sheer music listening.
If you want that, put on the ATs, or my Fostex RP40s, which will give you detail but not massive bass.

I find the ATs are better for classical, jazz, and watching streaming
stuff online or movies and such.

They're just not super musical, since they're intended as pro monitors.
They are excellent though for $55 studio cans.
However....

I'm difficult to please.

I still wanted more serious sized, bass-heavy but not distorted etc. headphones that were light and comfortable.
I heard the MDRX10s were exemplary in that mode.

You cannot find them retail in NY or LI where I'm at these days,
since Sony seems to be pushing their very basic BT headphones and sports buds and such, and nothing
"limited edition" like the X10s, which is very bloody annoying, so I ordered them up on Amazon from
my man BigBanana (sic) from out there in sunny Alameda, California.

He shipped these big bassy bastards
Priority Mail and they showed up fast.

I opened the package and held my breath, expecting to hear cheap
sounding sludgey cans that made Beats actually sound good.

Oh, how the mighty have risen.

I received mine today, 12/30/19, and thus far, they absolutely deliver what they promise.
In my experience this is a rarity for Sony these days, and a rarity for headphones in general.
I don't like Beats, don't think their quality is good enough to warrant the price, bass or not.

I've previewed Bose and they generally sound good, but kind of boring
and lifeless to my ears, with pleasant bass, but nothing truly outstanding, minus the high prices and
maybe noise-canceling if you absolutely need that.
I own Hifiman HE400I planar magnetics, which are the best open back headphones I own, they have nice solid tight bass, but not Deep DELICIOUS brain-eating bass.

Overall quality and detail, and high end, they beat these Sonys, but, on the other hand, the MDRX10s are stupendous for some decent clarity, they don't sound muddy at all, and, they pack a MASSIVE wallop in terms of bass response, impact, and bass clarity.

I would differentiate this way: The Hifiman HE400Is have a warmish, clear, detailed darkish signature with
tight, clean bass, and super detailed sparkling high end, but require a lot of amp power, whereas the MDRX10s offer high efficiency, super warm, muscular powerful bass response, with more of a sound signature that reminds me of great powered DJ monitors like KRK, JBL, or Pioneers with a good subwoofer added in.

You can also drive
the X10s with a phone or media player or tablet, without necessarily having to add a separate head. amp.
For really good quality 50mm bass-heavy headphones, that is a true accomplishment, without their losing
a lot of detail and quality in the mids and highs in the process.

Also, the bass on the X10s doesn't get
muddy or buzzy like those ghastly bass-adjustable Skullcandy Krushers that have a sliding bass switch on 'em.
Stay far away from those unless you like distorted bass in your drum and bass music.

I need only turn these bad boys up to maybe 10-12 on my PC Creative Labs amp setup, with some EQ,
to get a gorgeous loud but listenable level overall, with truly ass kicking bass for rock, dance music, etc.

After
about eight hours of testing, with a pair that was sent to me new, or open-box new, these headphones still
felt comfortable due to the soft on-ear pads, I wasn't expecting that, and, they deliver some serious performance,
easily 10x what I'd expected from them from reviews here or on YouTube.

I feel like Sony still makes quality stuff,
but mainly at their higher end, top shelf, but the X10s at roughly $90 that I paid for mine, easily punch way above their price point.

They seem to be well-made and are definitely comfortable, and even offer two removable
cables, and a nice vinyl metallic case.

They're quite lightweight, and look stylish and attractive without being
too garish.

They're spectacularly efficient headphones, even though they actually seem to offer a pretty
powerful, bass-emphasized signature, but still with some good clear mids and highs, and, the highs aren't
shrill or overbearing in any way.

This is highly important as I CANNOT STAND shrill, metallic, sibilant,
annoying unpleasant highs.

But I love me some good solid bass where the kick drum in say, the average
HD recording of The Police, (Voices Inside My Head) sounds like I'm putting my head about three feet or less
from the kick drum riser.

It doesn't sound like someone kicking the pedal against a rug, it sounds like
Stewart Copeland actually kicking that bloody pedal on that bloody kick drum.

Yes, these are better than Beats, by far, and they cost less, and they have more bass than many higher-end
headphones I could name (Grado?
Beyer?
AKG?
All great headphones that lack heavy bass).

That's about
all you need to know.

If you want budget-priced headphones with some unbelievable deep yet tight bass,
and clarity otherwise, and comfort, I can't recommend too many other headphones that fit the bill in a DJ
type design, that deliver all of the points I've mentioned.

I even own new PIoneer X7 DJ pro headphones,
and, honestly, I like the sound of the MDRX10s better, because, the Pioneers A. don't have as much good
bass as these do and B. they were a lot more money and C. they are spectacularly heavy, and not very
comfortable and D. the overall sound signature is a bit muddy, total V shape, murkier bass and highs
and not much good midrange at all.

They distort a lot more easily at higher volumes than the X10s.

So, Sony has redeemed themselves a bit this time out.

I figured I'd laugh at how awful they sounded,
and send them right back to Amazon, but, instead, I lucked out with a really bracing sounding pair
of headphones with 50mm drivers and bass that truly devastates.

I mainly listen to rock, pop, dance music,
goth, 80s, folk rock, power pop, etc., and metal.

The X10s are the perfect headphones for these genres.
If you want to listen to nothing but classical and jazz, I recommend the Hifimans, BeyerDynamics,
AKGs, Grados, etc.

As for the Sony MDRX10 "Simon Cowell but you needn't like him or his silly show to buy these": I recommend putting these through the best amplifier you own, EQing them to cut the regular bass down a tad and up the sub-bass a bit, and playing The Sisters Of Mercy's "Dominion/Mother Russia" at about volume 14, and be prepared for the retro nightclub playing in your head.
You have been warned for bass masturbation ecstasy dead ahead.

Pros & Cons -- a net win We've had our Circle for four months now.
If I had it to do over again, I'd still spend the money, but I wish it were better.

Note that Apple and Amazon parental controls are superior -- we block YouTube and the web browser on our children's phones and tablets.

Circle Pros:
- Fairly good at managing DNS & time limits
- Circle gives parents a targeted Internet “kill switch” for managed devices.
- Auto-enables Google Safe Search
- Good looking app
- Supports having unmanaged devices, thank goodness

Circle Cons:
- Abominable VPN.
The invasive mobile-client VPN isn’t nearly configurable enough.
It completely blocks use of WiFi at church and at school, because those networks don’t allow VPN and their networks are already locked-down.

So we don't use it, which means our children can hop on a neighbor's network and get unfettered access to the Internet... but we use Apple and Amazon parental controls to block YouTube and the web browser, so we'ere in a good spot.
- Sometimes circle blocks unmanaged devices, such as when it blocked iTunes on my wife's laptop from downloading a device update.

I had to turn of Circle, then it worked.
- The app logs me out unpredictably.
When I logged in, it said that I authenticated successfully, then sent me back to the login page.
I tried several times, with several failures, over a couple of days.

So I turned Circle off.
- No desktop management option.
Especially for initial configuration, I very much dislike being forced to use a tiny iPhone screen.

I’d much rather have a large monitor, a mouse and a keyboard.
- Auto-device naming stinks, and there's no search-by-MAC-address option.
We have a lot of devices -- kindle fires, kindle paper whites, iPhones, desktop computers, a smart TV, and so on.

When they all show up at once, and they're named unhelpfully "Amazon device", "Motorola device", and "Apple device", or even more obscure things, it makes it hard to figure out which device belongs in what profile.
It'd be so useful to be able to type in a partial MAC address to find the device and add it to a profile, but they don't offer that option.
Workaround: Change the WiFi password, and don't tell the children what it is for at least a few days.

Add devices to WiFi one or two at a time, then it's easier to figure out what they are, name them correctly, and assign them to the correct profile.
- Adding individual websites (rather than using preselected categories) is a pain, and it doesn’t always work.
- If you forget to unblock a profile, the child won't be able to use the internet.

It'd be super nice if blocking of a profile only lasted until the next morning -- then I wouldn't have to remember to unblock.
- Circle’s EULA is long, and not my favorite, but it's pretty much what I expect of the industry.
- Functions by doing DNS poisoning of the local network, so yes, there can be problems from time to time.

When something isn't working, turn off CIrcle, reboot the main router, and see if it starts working again.

The minuses: The speakers will be a bit of a process to remove to wash the headband.
The thickness of the material may make it too hot to wear for summer workouts.
The speakers aren’t in the ear, so for those who want to listen to their music a little louder, the people next to you will also likely hear it.

Overall: Perfect for me, especially for the price.
Might not be ideal for everyone.

The AX6000 boasts a 2.5Gbs speed WAN port.
That's your internet connection.
Who needs that even if it were true?
My CenturyLink DSL connection runs at a measly 30 Mbps.

Even a Cable One connection only runs at 100 Mbps.
Bottom line: If you already have an AC router don't waste your money on this.
If you're upgrading from an N class-- don't waste your money on this.

There are plenty of AC class routers available that are just as fast and less expensive.
And for Pete's sake don't fall for the special "gaming router" crap with the Star Trek design and a dozen antennas.
Might as well flush your dollars down the toilet.

Save Bucks and Buy a Watch That Sucks Spend a little more and buy a name brand watch!

I have had this watch for 9 months now, and feel that is sufficient time to have given it a fair shake.

Right out of the gate I had issues with watch integration.
Initially, they wanted me to have two apps on my phone- one to connect and one to track and display data.
The two apps, from the same company, didn’t work well with each other, let alone with iHealth or MyFitnessPal.
After some constructive feedback and some patience it seemed like they had fixed that.
At least with step and heart rate data, not sure about workout data.
But, that is fine, right?

I don’t my looking at cycling info with the Amazfit app- whatever.

So, merrily we roll along.
At some point I either stop caring or stop paying too close attention.
Every once in a while the watch needs rebooted.
Doesn’t all tech?

A good sign when it’s time to reboot is when you stop getting notifications.

Everything is fine.

My steps are being counted, my heart rate is monitored, I get text and email notifications, and I know when I’ve hit goal or I’ve been idle too long.

Then my charger breaks.
It didn’t stop charging, but one of the plastic wings broke off so I had to hold my watch to it with a rubber band until I could order a new charger.

No big deal, just another $10 to some other junk peddler.

I replaced my watch band also.

It seems that if you actually wear your watch, the watch band will wear- as will other wearable wares (ha ha, words).

Well, as luck would have it, today I start paying attention again.
I go to the Amazfit app, and find out that no data has been tracked since October!
Okay, maybe I just need to sync.
Syncing happens unusually fast this time.
Normally it takes a while.
Syncing complete and not only is two months of data not there, but the few steps this morning that are visible on the watch face are not there!
Alright alright.
I get that technology isn’t perfect.
I am close to this kind of thing in my work.
Unpair & pair the watch.

Of course, my steps from this morning are lost and unpairing almost acts like a factory reset (I say almost because I don’t exactly understand what it did, but it does allow restoration of settings from your account), but now my steps are syncing again.

Anyway, the moral of the story is that technology is sometimes more of a hindrance than a help...no, that can’t be right.
The moral is, don’t buy an off-brand device and expect it to work like a more expensive one.
(Tbh, my wife’s name brand watch was on sale and only slightly more expensive than this.)
Another moral is, don’t fool yourself into buying some substandard product because you are envious of what someone else has, or you have otherwise convinced yourself you need a trinket.

Another disappointment is that the location history only works with your phone.
Or at least mine does.
I put my tile on the outside of my car as i drove around town, marking it as lost in the am and asking for community locating help.

Anything, like being next to light or picking up light reflections from the siding, can make a difference.

It was not much good for recognizing a face from that angle.
I dropped the camera down to more eye level and now it will have great value of facial recognition.

They are pretty significant and it takes a week or more for the skin to heal up when it happens.
After some online searches, it turns out that this is a not uncommon problem.

I solved it by getting one of the metal link band replacements offered here on Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07KJYMZFM.

Phone integration for text and call notifications is spotty.

The other fitness features, like steps and move warnings.

GPS and heart rate tracking during bike rides.

Still Impressed- One Year Later (Edit) The positive reviews on these that sound like advertising are 100% legitimate because these absolutely deserve the attention.
Sound quality is easily comparable to headphones 3x the price of these.
The highs are crisp and clear and get better after a week of use once you get through the burn-in period.
The emphasis on the mids is amazing and something you can really have trouble finding on headphones these days.
The bass is full and heavy and definitely there without being too much and drowning the highs and mids.

Vocals are 11/10 if you ask me, and I listen to a lot of folk and other genres where vocals are the focal point.
So far comfort has been exceptional and I'm someone who often has trouble with headphones aching after only an hour.

I also ordered some aftermarket memory foam tips that improved comfort a lot but even with silicone, the fit is great.
I gave the sound cancelation a 4/5 only because they aren't active noise canceling and rely on the tips for sound cancelation.

Even without active cancelation, these are great at eliminating outside sounds.
Connection has been easy, although I have had trouble with the headphones automatically connecting out of the case.
This is pretty much a non-issue though as they connect quickly when you press the button on one of the two.

I've had no issues with range and can easily walk around the kitchen or room and listen seamlessly.
Overall, these are the best headphones in this price range for the value.

I'll update this review after I've used them for a few months.

EDIT: I'm still impressed with the audio quality but I've been having fairly severe connection issues.
I've consistently had issues from the getgo but they've been tolerable until recently.

As of today, especially (Feb 11, I bought these late December) the right headphone has been very glitchy and while watching youtube, consistently has a spotty connection and certain frequencies keep glitching in and out.
It was happening with music too.
If these headphones had reliable connectivity, they'd dominate the $100 range true wireless market.
Additionally, I've had plenty of issues with the headphones changing EQ and volume without warning.
It doesn't feel like an issue with my phone equalizer as these are the only headphones that do it.
They'll suddenly go from rich, deep, bassy sound and wonderful clarity to flat and bland mid-song.
I don't know what causes this.
As another top review stated, they seem to have better connectivity when the left headphone is connected to your source device.

I believe this is due to the left technically being the lead and so it does better with range and connection.

Honestly, I still recommend these and it may just be I got unlucky with mine.

Around 20 years ago when my parents got their first laptop, it actually came with fan for it.
It wasn’t nearly as cool as this one, but as soon as I got a laptop myself I wanted one.
Unfortunately, back when that happened I couldn’t find anything.
I figured I’d look to see if they had them available now and found this one!
I was originally worried because it only had one fan, but fan inside this is really powerful, at least for what it’s trying to accomplish.
My laptop used to sit on my lap or the bed and it would get pretty hot because of the lack of ventilation.

However this one fan is so powerful that even when the laptop has been on for hours, it’s still cool to the touch on the bottom.

The lights are rather cool, but I was incredibly glad that they came with an off button because they are really bright.
It would have been nicer if it had come with dimmer switch because I would have liked to be able to keep the lights on.
However the only adjuster it came with was a speed dial for the fan.
I pretty much keep it on full speed anyway so there was no point in having that on it, at least for my use.

Though I’m absolutely certain it would be a good thing for other users.

I also wish the prop system had better staying power.
If you move the laptop and fan up even minutely, whatever height you had set, automatically comes undone because there is nothing besides the large notch in the legs to grip onto.
Essentially, the only thing that keeps it on the notch you have it on is the weight of the laptop on top of it holding it down.

However, if you decide to move it or adjust where it’s sitting, you have to realign what level you had it propped at.

Overall, due mostly to the effectiveness and productivity of the fan, I do recommend this product.

I bought this card to replace my RX 570 graphics card hoping I would get a major boost in performance.

That hasn't been the case so far.
I have Windows 10 up to date, the right graphics card drivers, the right power supply, everything.
Everything is right in MSI Afterburner and power limit is set to +20.

But still this card performs worse than my RX 570 at times, I'll be playing and my Core Clock frequencies will be all over the place, dropping to as low as 300mhz for no reason then spiking back up to 1750mhz, then up and down over and over again.
No matter what I lock the frequency to,  it still will go all over the place.
This makes the frames rates range from 10-165 FPS and it creates massive stutters.
I've done everything I can to get this card working properly it still, nothing.

Definitely wouldn't recommend as of now.

(Edit)
I bought a replacement card and got the same result.
I think I found the problem and I'm pretty sure it has to do with the VRM's (Voltage Regulator Modules) and a bad cooling configuration.
Every time I start up a game, it seems to do fine, only for a minute or so.
It starts off by running at it's intended frequency and proper power supply voltage, then GPU frequencies and power supply usage will drop drastically, then go back up and down again.
These issues can be caused by overheating of the VRM's, which explains why my GPU's back plate gets unreasonably hot after only a few minutes of gaming.

I guess I shouldn't be surprised though since the RX 5700's older brother (RX 5700 XT) from XFX got bad reviews from critiques because of bad cooling, and both cards look similar when it comes to the heating configuration.

During calls you also use this to hangup.

I found this feature useful, although they are very sensitive, if you adjust the buds in your ear you may accidentally hangup or skip to the next track.

- Phone Calls: sound is clear on both sides.
Compared to AirPods, my caller was not able to notice a significant difference on their side.

Starting with Pros/Cons

Pros:
+Name recognition.
Bose makes good headphones.

These earbuds deliver music as crisp as you'd expect from Bose.
+Cheaper than paying for hearing aides if you are borderline on needing them.
+Noise cancelling/amplification.
It works.

But settings are limited.

Cons:
- Short battery life.

On full charge I got only around 2.5 to 3 hours of maximum use before having to take them off and recharge.
-Bulky and cumbersome.

The collar ring is not flexible in any way to ergonomically lay flat to your neck.
- Earbud wires are too short.
Every time I turned my head the wires would pull the earbuds out of place.

Either look straight ahead or get used to readjusting the fit in each ear.
- Constantly opening the control app.
The app has to be fully open to adjust any settings.

Having to change settings constantly for varying volumes was a huge hassle.
- Documentation.

It is sorely lacking any detail.

Why I rated as I did:

I bought a pair of Bose Hearphones to try and combat a very specific sort of noisy environment: attending competitive Irish dance events.

When hundreds of dancers are all performing hard shoe routines on 8+ wooden stages inside a gym/arena with live musicians (fiddle or accordion) accompanying them, the cacophony of sounds is often deafening and painful to me.

But my daughter dances and loves it, so I needed to try something.

Do the Hearphones work?
Technically, yes.
The ability to set input between 360 degree, 180 degree (front) or 70 degree (direct front) focal areas is a nice feature.
However - to amplify voices the Hearphones also amplify all surrounding sounds.
To cancel out excess sound, voices are also cancelled out.
The middle ground setting was no better than going without them.
This was not clearly explained anywhere.

I learned through a long day of trial and error.

Further the audio app needed to control the settings has to be open for every adjustment.
There is no lock screen option for quick adjustments.
While watching my daughter dance - with excess sound dialed out - I had to look down and adjust the settings to hear my wife or friends talking.

And at the level I could easily hear them, the hearphones were again passing all sounds through in an amplified state making a loud environment worse.

By the end of the day I had a migraine and was left frustrated at how limiting the settings were.

The ability to selectively cancel (some/all) excess sound while still passing voices through is what I was looking for.
In the situation I need these to help me, they do not.

Older Silverado door tweeters If you have an older Silverado (2003 vintage) with door tweeters, these will work if you have a 2" hole saw.
The stock tweeters are mounted in a oval shaped bracket held with two metal nuts.
Pull out the bracket, carefully break out the stock tweeter, then drill a 2" hole right where the stock tweeter was.
Use the included saw-tooth ring to slightly increase the diameter of the new tweeter.

Apply super glue around the perimeter of the new tweeter, place it in the new hole, and clamp or weight it down until the glue dries.
I then cut the plug off of the old tweeter leaving about 3" of wire and soldered it to the new tweeter wire, also cut to about 3".
As I recall, the blue wire of the stock tweeters is positive.
Put the bracket back in place, plug in the electrical, and you are done.

Amazon, Please Fix FireTV OS Let me preface this by saying I was an early adopter of FireTv.
I have been on board since the beginning and have owned at least 1 of every version of FireTV device (except the new Gen 2 Cube).
For the most part I have loved these devices, especially my 2 FireTV Cubes.
That is, until October of 2019, about the time Amazon started making major changes to FireTV OS.

Until that time, these were definitely 5 star devices.

My issues started in October (I think).
It also has affected my FireTv 4k stick, FireTv 4k pendant, etc.
These devices have become very buggy since Amazon started upgrading FireTv OS.
Cubes randomly freeze or close apps.
Very slow response (sometimes).
CEC stopped working on 4k stick.
I have to restart the devices regularly.
None of these issues existed prior to the OS "upgrades".
I'm really shocked at how badly these upgrades have been managed.
What was a great device (devices) has become a crap-shoot of sorts.
When will the device freeze?
When will I have to power cycle it?
Because I know it will happen.
If I had only 1 FireTv device, I would have definitely thought I was having hardware issues.

But no, ALL my Fire TV devices have been affected, but none more than the FireTV cubes.

I don't want to completely change my electronics ecosystem.
I love being able to turn lights on/off via voice.
Or playing music.
My grandkids thought it was so cool Alexa could turn on the Christmas tree lights.

But right now the main function as an audio/video controller is severely compromised.

Oh, and while you are busy fixing FireTV OS, please add FandangoNow and VUDU to the appstore.
I have a large online video library and unfortunately it is impossible to have one app contain all of my movies due to movie studio rights.
So do us devoted Amazon users a solid and make life easier by adding these apps.

Most motherboards are particular about the brand and type of RAM that is being used.

Pros:
-Seems good quality construction
-Super Easy to setup, connect and go
-No apparent compression
-It works great for movies, presentations, pictures and other stuff with a low frame rate.
-When it gets hot it disconnects till it gets cool, this is good in the sense that it just doesn't burn or melts, they have a failsafe so it's something.
-Can be used with something with highish framerate if you strap it to a fan

Cons:
-Gets hot when you push it, I was using it for Zwift (kind of a video game) and it would get hot and disconnect leaving you stranded for minutes.
-There is signal degradation with high bit rate movies (when there is too much going on on the screen, like a car chase)
-Doesn't activate Samsung Dex or desktop mode on android phones, just does screen mirroring.

Conclusion, it works, but is not meant for heavy duty usage, has poor heavy heat management, but at least it has overheat protections in place which prevent it from burning, and you can ducttape it, to a cooling fan and it works great that way.

The signal degradation issues are inherent to this kind of devices, even if the signal is totally uncompressed is a digital signal and data is lost along the way, specially with obstructions or electrical/static noise (which we all have with so many wireless crap around us) or if the frame rate is high, there is only so much data that makes it thru and you start seeing artifacts and pixelation all over the place.

Don't get me wrong, is very usable, I'm very picky so this whole thing is very very subjective, for movies is only in some parts where you can see issues, but for the most part, it looks like your regular Netflix stream, for games it craps out a bit, but hey at least I don't have to run a 5meter/15ft cable across my room and into the drywall so there is that.

If you want to show pictures, movies or a presentation and you have a direct line of sight between the transmitter and receiver this thing is great I tested it to 10 meters/30ft (ran out of room) and still worked flawlessly.

So again, the whole thing is very subjective depending on what is good picture quality for you.

I'm still debating whether to keep it, mostly cause I hate having to cool it down, the fan is just an extra thing I have to connect to another usb port which I hate.

If it didn't had that issue I wouldn't mind the slight picture degradation that it gives while gaming or when Michael Bay is blowing too much stuff up and trying to get you dizzy by spinning and shaking the camera all over the place.

Perfect for those who just want a solid, reliable, quiet and simple mouse Today's mice try to do it all, and thus have many buttons and settings.

That makes sense if you use a mouse for "real work" as well as gaming, but for those of us who are minimalist and need a wireless mouse to simply BE a get-it-done mouse, those do-it-all mice are overkill (and overly expensive).
If this describes your need--a mouse that does the simple mouse functions--this mouse is perfect.
It has only two buttons and a scroll wheel (which is a third button).
No extraneous buttons in the thumb-rest, no choices to make.
It is very comfortable with a very "grippy" textured rubber surface that gives it a very secure feel in the fingers, especially for finer movements.
(The arch might be a little low and not sit right in your palm if you have larger hands.)

And, as the name implies, the buttons are very quiet when depressed; just a soft tap sound.

Another blessing (for minimalists like me) is that it is NOT a Bluetooth mouse.
It uses a very small USB dongle and the wireless connection is very solid.
Unlike with Bluetooth (BT), there is no lag in transmission (which sometimes occurs), or interference with other BT devices or weirdness getting the BT to connect.
Absolutely, some people need BT, particularly if they want to use the device on more than one device.
And, it is true you tie up a USB port, but often a good keyboard will have an extra one or two USB slots, and/or there are USB hubs.
(The major drawback would be if you used this with a computer such as the newer MacBooks that only have type C ports.
Then, you would need an adapter for the USB A style dongle, which becomes unwieldy.

In that scenario, a BT wireless mouse is better.)

LogiTech claims a batter life of two years.
If by chance I'm still around and remember, I'll update this post in two years and let you know!

But at the low price of this mouse (less than twenty at time of purchase in 2019) even if the entire device only lasts two years, it's a bargain.

In sum, if you need a wireless right-handed USB (not BT) mouse with nothing more than basic functions that feels great, is very quiet, and is at a bargain price, look no further.

Best mount I've ever installed...well worth the $$ I've mounted probably a dozen TVs and in brick and drywall (with and without studs) - each with a different mount bracket - and ECHOGEAR's is the best quality and easiest to mount I've ever used.

Here's why:

- Comes with a mounting template (missing, strangely, from so many other brands) that makes hole positioning a breeze.
- Comes with every assortment of mounting bolt under the sun for attaching your television to the mount.
- Has tilt adjustment in the bracket (think "roll axis" of a plane) so, despite my OCD driving me to mount it as level as possible, I can still tweak it once mounted.
- Massive range of positioning for swiveling your TV to left or right, and very smooth articulation for repositioning once mounted (which with this one we do regularly).
- Large spacing in the mount plate so if you're running wires in the wall it can accommodate even double-sized panels sitting within the open spaces of the mount plate.
- Accommodates a crazy range of TV sizes, good for future-proofing!
Worth considering: the 42"-85" mount is quite heavy at just over 25 lbs.
Combine this with it's size and it may be tough for some to install solo.

In my case, as soon as I had one lag bolt partially in a stud it was like having a second helper (that bolt could support one side while I did the other) but you may want a hand for just the first bolt.

That said, the weight is indicative of the build quality.

I'm pretty sure I'll never buy a different brand mount again.
This one is just too good and was so easy to install, especially considering the sub-$100 price.

Anyways, if you have the drop problem, or you can't get to the admin page at 192.168.100.1 (best indicator of an issue, AFAICT), try leaving the modem unplugged for 15 minutes or so and plug it back in.

I had drops every 4 hours on the dot, but if the admin page was still accessible 1 hour after booting, it would be stable until the next power outage.

Seems that power cycling too quickly puts it into an unstable state.
Don't waste your time with this, but if you have no other options, try the above.
If 15 minutes doesn't work, try overnight.
But really, just buy a used CM500 for 20 bucks unless you need 3.1.

Great performance, for a premium company the mounting could be improved.
I only bought this because my Prolimatech Megahalems did not support AM4 and they had no updated mounting hardware for it.
Decided to go with a company that appears to future support their coolers which Noctua does from what I have read.
The box, packaging and instructions all are top notch quality.
Once I read through the instructions I figured it would mount rather well being the price and quality of company behind it.
Once I installed the support bars I placed the cooler down and prepared to tighten the last 2 main attachment screws.
It took me a few minutes of pressing the screwdriver down trying for the threaded portion to catch.
I simply tried to start the threads on one side with only a few turns to get it to catch but then on the other side I could not get it to grab on.
I finally got the threads to start and it screwed down fine from there.
My previous cooler is NIGHT AND DAY better mounting, it uses basically the same style of mount but the quality is SO much better on the Prolimatech.
You simply place the cooler on the cpu just like the Noctua but then the two final screws easily hand thread into position without any force or stress to get them started.
Then you take a screw driver and can easily and carefully tighten each side down a little by little till fully tight.
Yes this Noctua worked but the mounting style is far inferior to what I have been using these last 8 or so years.
The cooling performance in the benchmarks show the Noctua does cool a few degrees better than my previous cooler which is nice considering my disappointing view of the install.
Yes the mount system works and sure plenty of people got theirs to thread in on the first try, that still does change my opinion on the much better designs out there.

Last this Noctua 14 cooler keeps my stock AMD 2700x at around 40c-45c while gaming.

I bought better coolers for a few reasons.
1.)

Keep the CPU cooler for ease of possible overclocking
2.)

Less noise with better heatsink and lower fan speed
3.)
Less force required in installation, easier to get the thermal compound the way you want when installation is simple.
In the past heavy force had to be applied always risking damage to hardware.

Some coolers really make on/off of the cooler a pleasant experience.

#3 is why this cooler got a 4 out of 5.
It's a great cooler from appears to be a great cooler company.
They need to look around and see what out premium cooler companies have done.
I truly wish there would have been a adapter kit for my old Megahalems as not only was it very close in performance but mount is a 10 out of 10.
I would rate the Noctua mount 7 out of 10.

Best Value Under $50 Pros:
Low price.
Room for full size components.
Clean, basic aesthetics.
Tempered glass side panel.
Room for cable management behind motherboard tray.
Full length power supply shroud.
Filters for front and top fan mounts and bottom power supply mount.
Excellent airflow.
Ample front I/O.

Cons:
Front panel connectors a bit short for full size ATX boards, depending on connector location.
Front fan filter clipped in to front panel, very difficult to remove for cleaning.
Bottom power supply fan filter very flimsy.
Power supply shroud cutouts for cables very small/awkwardly placed - a third cutout closer to the rear panel would have been a huge help.
CPU power connector cutout not large enough for 8 pin connectors with motherboard installed.

Not an issue for 4+4 pin connectors.

Notes:
Sheet metal is fairly thin - rear panel is easily bent if force is applied.
PCIe slot covers are breakaway style, rather than replaceable.
Front of case has a 5.25" bay cutout, and another 5.25" breakaway cover below it, but the front panel only has room for one 5.25" bay, and the case only has mounting points for one bay.

Seems to be re-used tooling from an older case.

Overall, this is clearly a budget case, and some corners were cut to get it down to this price point while including the glass side panel.
I do not feel the cut corners take anything away from the overall appeal or value proposition of the case, but they should be noted.

A couple basic changes could significantly improve this case in terms of compatibility with more hardware: a slightly larger EPS power cutout, a third cutout in the PSU shroud close to the rear panel, a front cutout running across the PSU shroud (and a [re]movable HDD cage) to allow for 360mm radiator mounting, and slightly longer front IO cables would make this a no-brainer in any build.

Overall, would highly recommend to anyone looking for a case under $50, intend to use it again for additional budget builds.

Had issues with my wraith, this was a great replacement I had been having fan noise issues with my wraith cooler, it would often produce a lot of fan noise at higher fan speeds, it seemed like a bad bearing.

I am thinking about getting another to throw on my FX-9370 system since it has a extremely high TDP requirement that not a lot of cooling solutions can meet.

The Skullcandy Skull crushers are bad!
Their sound quality are of $30 headohones, they get all the attention due to their silly fake bass sliding gimik, please don't fall for it.

But they do have excellent battery life and good built quality.

The V-moda Crossfade wireless were the closest ones that got to the Sony's.
Excellent built quality, great looks and built quality, loud volume, good enough bass, but not Sony's level, Sony's level of bass is the maximum you can get while still have excellent mids.
Vmoda has 75% of Sony's bass and excellent bass as well.
The deal with the vmoda were that they're INCREDIBLY tight on your head and after 1hr your ears will be aching!

The battery life was also very poor.
Keep in mind I listen to my music at high volume so the battery will not last as what it's advertised on the box, but the Sony will easily go two plus weeks if not three weeks without needing to be charged.
Unfortunately returned the vmodas.
I think I'll buy them again in the future when they have folding ear cups, not as tight and better battery because their sound is excellent!

Now down the the Beats Studio 3s, these are pretty good, and I ended up keeping them, not because they're as good as the Sony's, but they do everything at B+ at least.
- Loud volume
- great bass
- great battery
- fast charging

Cheap built quality so I know it'll break soon, so I wear it at the office, not at the gym, Evey review warns you that it'll eventually break and I can see why, it's super thin and plasticy.
The mids not as good as the Sony's or vmodas, but they're very comfortable and have the best sound isolation compared to all others, which is why it's good for the office.

The most disappointing unfortunately has been the JBL Under Armour Sport Train Wireless( The Rock's Headohones)
They look and feel excellent, they have thought of many things synch as pass thru feature and fast charging but holy moly they get the major stuff wrong.
- no where loud enough with Bluetooth or wired

Vmodas mids, with Sony's bass and volume.
Sony's battery
Fast charging of Beats
The sound isolation of the Beats Studios 3s
Sporty looks of the JBL

Fantastic sound in a small and beautifully designed package If you're trying to get a budget 5.1, this system is actually really fantastic when the price point is under $200.

I did a lot of research before I bought these and needed something specific, these checked off the list perfectly.

The design is beautifully minimal with the satellites and speakers featuring all black details.
The only branding is the ELAC logo on the metal grille, which you can barely see.
The subwoofer matches the styling from ELAC’s Andrew Jones designed higher end line.

This is probably the only piece in the set that has a clear brand name with its embossed ELAC branding in dark silver.

I tested the ELAC CINEMA 5 system running off a DENON S750H AVR in Surround with lots of different content.

The system is setup in my living room that measures approx 10x12’ with high ceilings.

I tested the system with the following media:

Films and shows: Star Wars: The Force Awakens, The Witcher, Our Planet.

Video games on the PS4 such as God of War, Spider-man, Jedi: Fallen Order.

Music ranging from Latin, Jazz, trap, hip-hop, house, techno, and mid-range to bass heavy music.

It's a satellite based sound system, so you need to accept that the midrange and low-end of the satellites will not compare to the bookshelf-type speakers that most audiophile forums/posters/etc will recommend all the time...but that’s perfectly fine in this use case.

Everything coming out of the satellites is super clear and crisp, but as they don't have deep mids or lows the subwoofer picks up those frequencies.

If you have your sound setup properly via your AVR this will be seamless and sound perfect.

The subwoofer is pretty beefy sound wise even at 100 watts PEAK RMS.
Is it as powerful or detailed as a studio sub which can go down to 23hz?
No, of course not.
But you're not buying it for that.

Yes it doesn't go below 40hz, but neither do a lot of subs at this price point (go look, you won't find any decent ones that do).

Footsteps from an alien in Star Wars: The Force Awakens sounded clear and defined.

The hum of Thano's spaceship in Avengers: Endgame makes you feel like you're on board (I had a 250 watt sub from another HTIB before that didn't have this definition), and music bumps with clear definition between the kick and sub-bass.

With that said, it's really good for the price point and will shake your apartment.

Here's the other thing, as I said before it also comes down to how you tweak your sound settings in your AVR.
Nothing will sound amazing by default on any speaker unless you optimize.

With the right settings on your AVR this system will sound great in your room.

Construction is solid, no rattling or vibration.

The satellites and subwoofer have a hefty weight but are minimal and clean.

**Here's who should get the system:**

You have an apartment or small area with limited space but you want better sound than a sound bar

You want a 5.1 setup to use with an AVR and don't want to shell out a lot of money for absurdly oversized "bookshelf" speakers

You want small satellites for your surrounds

You can't convince yourself to pay 500+ for a Sound bar system

You don't want to pay 1500+ for a sound bar that has "virtual" Surround Sound and Atmos for your apartment.

You want something elegantly designed and discrete that doesn’t take a lot of space.

**Who shouldn't get this system:**

People with large spaces, specifically large dens or living rooms in a house where you need to cover a lot of space.

If you want full-range sound from your fronts.

Small satellites will never give that to you, just a fact.

You want beefy big speakers.

These are discrete and small.

Atmos Out of the box (you can add heights or Atmos enabled speakers later if you want and if you have an Atmos friendly AVR).

You can even use these satellites for Atmos height speakers if you really wanted to.

You want really articulate bass that goes really, really deep.

You'll need to shell out minimum $200 just for the Sub to get that.

**Bottom Line**

Time will tell how long these last and other factors, but out of the box, hooked up and tweaked to the right settings they sound amazing and exactly fit my needs.

Just understand that you are not going to get full-range sound from the satellites (you will with the whole system combined and optimized for your room).
If that's what you're looking for then you simply need bigger speakers with a larger frequency range.

At that point your fronts ALONE without a center channel will cost as much as this system (at the current price of $139).

If you want a compact and amazing sounding 5.1 surround system at a great price point, grab these when they’re under $200.

The biggest trouble I had with cheaper models was people complaining about me being too quiet or sounding strange, but with this model I haven't heard any complaints yet.
It pairs just fine with my GXV3240, though to get it to work I had to disable handsfree mode, which was counter-intuitive.

One thing that is very convenient is if you have it off your head, and you hear the phone ringing, the headset will sense somehow when you put it back on it and answer the call without you having to press the button.

The only caveat is the GXV3240 driver only has partial support with this model, so that I can only use it receive calls, not to place them.
So if I really want to use this for an outgoing call, rather than the handset, I have to call my customer on another company line, and transfer the call back to my SIP phone.

Useful for entertainment I purchased four "Echo show 5" units.
One was for my personal use and the other three I gifted them to family members.
The echo show 5 works great.

It is user friendly and provides easy to follow instructions to connect it to the internet.
I am assuming that the developers' intentions were to use it as an entertainment piece.
As such it works perfect.

However reading about its features, I decided that I could use it as a tool to help aging family members.
The two units were used in the US to communicate with an elderly family member who is located about 65 miles away.
She is using it as a clock (an expensive clock).

Also, in the event that she needs assistance to contact a family member by asking Alexa to dial the family member's phone number.
We practiced a few times, so I hope that if it is needed, she will be able to use it.
The other two units were taken overseas with the hope that they could be used in a similar manner.
Before I purchased the units I did not research the languages that the software is able to speak.
When I was setting mine up, I scrolled through the language features and realized that Greek was not one of them.
So, I set it up for English.
The family member in the US speaks broken English so she can use it.

The other family members in Greece speeks fluent English but the elder parent speaks no English.
Again, no complaints because the unit is not advertised as a medical allert aid or a product to be used for elderly people as a means of comunication.

Although it has enough features that the developers could ensure that the software could be utilized for elderly or disabled individuals.
In case anyone is interested the Echo products in general do work great in Greece.

You can get information about the local weather, the time and other local and international features in the same manner as if you were to use it in the United States.
I have not been able to set it up to use the "drop in" feature or the feature to call land lines or cell phones.
I hope that other developers look at the Echo Show 5 product and get inspired to develop a product that can be utilized by the elderly and disable populations.

Amazon engineers do indeed try to curb this problem by including several sliders that keep the wires together and a place on the mount where the wires can be fed through, but it isnt quite enough to alleviate the problem.
These few things aside, the echo auto is amazing.
Its just as quick and effective as my home echos.
Also, it allows me to control things in my home and use the intercom and announcement features while out on the go.
I could feasibly do all these things with my phone, but not with my voice and certainly not while driving.
If you can overlook the issues I listed above, this product will satisfy your smart car desires.

Surround Sound is Inconsistent: Here's How to Fix It Topline: Great room filling sound, but to avoid distortion and dropped connections, you have to use ethernet cables on every device in your console to avoid interference--to which the soundbar is obscenely susceptible.
Out of box and with a bunch of wireless components nearby, you'll be banging your head against a wall.
The sound quality *is* fantastic, but the documentation is either wrong, misleading, or incomplete.
(I recommend you look at the manuals available on the website to see what I mean.)
Additionally, the Vizio SmartCast app is incredibly finicky, particularly when it comes to recognizing your device.
Which wouldn't be a problem if it weren't for the fact that the Vizio remotes are just difficult to use (why don't they backlight the VERY DARK, VERY SMALL LCD screen on them?).
Finally, the Subwoofer is huge.
HUGE.
Doublecheck its measurements to make sure you can accommodate it in your space.

(And make sure you have a power outlet near your couch.)

INTERFERENCE/SURROUND DISTORTED/DROPPED:

The problem with the SB46514-F6 is that the signal it sends to the subwoofer is prone to interference.
I know this because it was plagued with "popping" distortion, disappearing voices, and dropped surround.
Attempting to reproduce the effect was hit-or-miss.
Sometimes I just needed to return to a menu and then re-start a video.
Sometimes I needed to re-pair the subwoofer (a ridiculously laborious process).

But the repair wouldn't last: Soon, the popping and dropping resurfaced.

On one forum, a user mentioned marginal improvement by *turning the subwoofer around* so its rear faced the soundbar (and away from the power strip it was close to).

I tried it, and indeed, the sound cut out less frequently--it seems the receiving circuitry on the subwoofer is in the back.

So, I deactivated the wireless on pretty much all of my peripherals.
I wired all the connections in the media console--from my TV, to my PS4, to my AppleTV--and deactivated all wifi components except the router.

With that, I achieved seamless, uninterrupted surround sound.

I won't attempt a teardown of the soundbar to get into the details, but my theory is that the soundbar concentrates its antennae all together on the left side, away from the power supply to avoid electrical interference.
But it has several antennae for a few purposes.
You're bound to get interference.
It appears to have Bluetooth, some variety of NFC antenna, a wifi antenna, and another radio antenna that carries the signal to the subwoofer.
That's four, in one small enclosure.

If it's under your wifi activated tv, and near your wifi activated (and bluetooth remote-controlled) apple tv, and all by your router, that's just a lot of potential for interference.

DOCUMENTATION:

The quick start guide is a decent walkthrough, and the manual has some useful tips, but the language is ambiguous about whether you can get ATMOS sound from any device routed through your TV, or if it needs to be plugged directly into your soundbar's ARC HDMI port.
(My understanding: You need to be plugged directly into the ARC HDMI port, and it may work with a hub that passes 4k through as well.)
Does HDMI-CEC need to be on?
Yes!
Kind of.

But additional documentation is maddeningly hard to find: The distortion issue seems to be a crisis for Vizio, to the point they've attempted to roll out new firmware (enjoy updating it using the SmartCast app, which is awful in this venture).

But nowhere do they acknowledge the reality of interference.

REMOTE:

Hard to see.
No backlight.

Dark screen.

SMARTCAST APP:

Takes a number of different approaches to identifying your soundbar, insists on putting your soundbar on wifi at first, requires you to place your phone on it for some reason, sometimes doesn't detect it, and once set up, doesn't detect the soundbar in subsequent uses.
(Even after deleting and going through the process again.)
Its most consistent reliability comes when the soundbar is hardwired into the router.
Additionally, if you want to check settings, it *still* requires you to request them through the app, and then the speaker... says them to you.

Out loud.

SOUND:

It's great.
Really and truly: If you can get it to work properly, you'll love it, and your neighbors will hate you.
My only complaint sound wise is that the sound doesn't seem to go very low before totally cutting out.

Checked here and there, and found the solution (unfortunately not here), and sharing it with you as a New Year Gift ( if you decide to buy me a beer, I would accept :) )
So the solution of low sound coming form your new surround speakers is to install on your phones a Bose Mobile app.
There are few.

"Bose Connect" and "Bose Music" will not work with soundbar 300, they do with 500/700.
For soundbar 300 model you need "Bose SoundTouch" app.
It works using your home Wi-Fi to connect your phone/app with the soundbar.

To prepare your soundbar for connection, press your soundtouch button on your remote, then press and hold 9.
Open the app and follow instructions.
It will also check for updates ( I even didn't know this sound system could get updates, so did it for a first time in 2 years since I bought it.

Update took a while, about 15 minutes).
When you are connected, on app under settings you could find "Audio Settings".

There you can adjust the Central Level and your Surround Level, last one is what is bothering you, hit it to 10 :) Test your sound now.

Best For 14 gauge Or Larger Wire.
Stay Away For Smaller Wire.
I have a 7.1 system with 16 gauge wire running to all 7 of my speakers.
The way these plugs clamp down on the bare wire requires fanning out the wire and then screwing the plug together.

The problem is that 16 gauge wire and most certainly anything smaller than 16 gauge wire pulls right out of the plug after it's screwed together, there's just not enough thickness where the teeth of the plug clamp down on the wire.
I overcame this by twisting the wire end like you normally would to put it into a binding post style connector, and just bending it over like that inside the banana plug.
It still doesn't feel like a great connection, but it doesn't easily pull out, although it will with a moderate force tug.
If you're using 14 gauge or larger wire I would buy these without hesitation, because them seem well made.

It comes with the add-a-circuit kit and you don't need to buy anything else to hardwire your dash cam.

Recommended tools: plier, clean cloth, multi-meter, electrical tape

Workflow:

1.

Check the fuse box, and figure out which fuse is hot (feeds power even when the engine is turned off) by using the multimeter.

2.

Attach the black wire to the metal chassis first, secure it.

3.

Attach the red wire to the always-hot fuse with the add-a-circuit one.

4.

Plug the USB to your dash cam to make sure you get the power when the engine is off.

That's it.
I managed to install the setup within 30 minutes the first car then 15 minutes the second one.
I highly recommend this kit to everyone. :)

Great sounding Hi-Fi Music!
If you like Alexa automation and want something a bit more affordable to use with your own speaker system, this may be a good option.
But this is only as good as what you connect it to.
That being said, I have it connected to my Sony HT-NT5 sound-bar system with subwoofer which is a good sounding system, not an audiophile’s first choice but nonetheless a decent system.
I connected the Echo Link to the sound bar via an optical audio cable and turned the Echo Link volume all the way up.
I was not expecting anything great but what I get is really good.
Clear Hi-Fi audio with no distortion.
Much much better than what comes out of any Echo speaker or connecting an Echo speaker to external sound system via 3.5mm cable.
I control the volume through my sound-bar remote.
Or you can use Alexa for that too but she can only get the volume as high as what the sound-bar is set to.
So I tell my Alexa Echo-Dot to play Beats 1 on Apple music and she sends the music to the Link.
All I have to do is make sure my sound-bar is on and select the correct input.
I was skeptical at first because of some not-so-good reviews but I'm quite satisfied with the Link.
I’m sure there are much better high-end options and if I have it connected to a super high end system, the quality will be better.
Just don't think you're going to get great sounding audiophile standard Hi-Fi music with this Link especially if you connect it to a subpar speaker system.

Bought for my Mom My mom is pretty hard to buy for.
But this last time I visited I knew this might be a great gift.
Everytime I visit her we watch a little tv and the volume is always going up and down to accommodate her aging ears.
I wasn't sure if it was a gimmick or not - but they have a 30 day return so I thought I'd give it a go.
This was replacing an LG soundbar that didn't solve the her hearing issue.
Setting it up was pretty easy - there is unfortunately no HDMI, I knew that before buying however.

Once it was set up I could tell the difference instantly, the voices were much clearer and this was on the lowest boost (AC1) - My mom asked me what I thought and I stressed to her what matters is what she thinks.
I was able to stay for a couple days after setting it up.
We pretty quickly bumped it to AC2, and turned on the sound leveling.
Right now it's on AC3.

I don't know any other way to say this... each increase of the AC level makes it sound less hi-hi / theater like to my ears but again, that's not the point.

The first evening with AC set to one, Sound leveling Off, and Surround set to 1 (we never changed the surround level), We barely touched the volume, but she did mention how some things were loud - So I turned on the sound leveling, which definitely impacts the 'theater quality' and bumped the AC to level 2.
My Brother came over and he too immediately noticed the difference, commenting that is sounded clear and much better than the old sound bar.
Yet there where still a few times we played with the volume so I bumped the AC to level 3. and this is where it was when I left.
This soundbar has 6 levels for accuvoice, Zvox makes soundbars with just AC on or off...
I wonder what level the is equivalent to?

In the end we watched TV with the sound on '11' which was *maybe* one level higher than I would have listened, certainly not as loud as my Mom used to listen at, and with her hearing more of the content.

The remote was quite a bit nicer than I expected, but Mom won't be needing it as the soundbar can learn your TVs Power, Volume up, Volume down, and Mute and respond to them.
This is one spot where the documentation fails slightly - For one thing the directions for setting this up are not included I had to download them...

Oh and a side note, they brag about the one page of directions - yes they are one page, one very large page printed on both sides and folded six times (yeah, marketing people) - Anyhow back to the programming the sound bar to respond to your TV - you need to download the directions from there website. and then the directions won't work, it simply will not enter 'learning' mode.
Well the missing detail from the direction is the sound bar must be OFF at the beginning of the setup.
It didn't take me long to figure that out, but it should have been clearly stated.

(I did try it a few times using first the remote then the physical buttons before discovering it needed to be OFF first - at which point the remote or the physical buttons worked)

So in short - super happy - it sounds great, it does sound better with the AC lower and the sound leveling off, but it still sounds great as i configured it for my mom - and that was the whole point.
Does my mom hear every word now?

no - But we can watch tv quieter than we used to, and we adjust the volume significantly less then before (like 90% less)

We are thinking of getting this sound bar for my mother-in-law as well.
And I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it for anyone that is looking at getting a sound bar in general.

Personally, I have a Marantz AV receiver and lots of speakers - but for a sound bar this thing sounds great - and better than the $150ish sound bar we got from the big box store.
